title: Treasurer defends inflation record as 15-year interest rate high looms
text:
On the eve of a widely anticipated rate hike that would push interest rates to their highest level in 15 years, the treasurer has defended the government's track record on inflation, saying high petrol prices are to blame rather than government spending.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers confirmed the budget deficit for last financial year was $6 billion better than the $28.3 billion forecast in May.

He said that showed the government had been "limiting spending growth" and doing the work to curb inflation ahead of the Reserve Bank's looming decision on Tuesday whether to again hikes the official cash rate to a possible 4.6 per cent.

The last time the cash rate was around this level was October to November 2011, meaning anyone who has purchased their first home since that time has never had to service a higher borrowing level on their loan.

Mr Chalmers revealed the projected national debt was lower than forecast in the May budget, with health costs and other payments down $1.4 billion and revenue up $4.6 billion more than expected.

The increased tax was driven by better-than-expected returns on superannuation investments, rather than a higher take from wage earners or mining revenue, the latter which came in short on budget forecasts.

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher credited the budget savings to less spending across aged care, childcare and the pharmaceutical benefits scheme (PBS).

Households brace for interest rate hike

The treasurer pushed back on suggestions the government could do more to help households, pointing to global economic pressure and the Iran-US war as "absolutely disastrous" for family budgets in Australia.

While Mr Chalmers celebrated an improvement for the budget, he conceded that there would be "difficult months" ahead.

When will the RBA stop raising rates? The Reserve Bank is meeting tomorrow for the sixth time this year, and both financial markets and economists think it is almost certain it will raise interest rates for the fourth time.

He insisted other countries were in a "far worse position" than Australia, and said anybody who had watched recent developments in global debt and bond markets would understand they were having a "very serious pressure" on borrowing costs.

The figures released on Monday showed government spending had risen from 26.6 per cent to 26.9 per cent of GDP, largely reflecting the weaker economic growth of the Australian economy.

Mr Chalmers insisted the war in the Middle East, not government spending, was to blame for increasing inflation.

"Any objective observer of what's happening in our economy and particularly what's happening with inflation, will conclude that a big driver of the inflation we're seeing in our economy right now comes from the Middle East," he said.

But Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the announcement was a "desperate attempt to distract Australians from the prospect of three more interest rate rises".

He said the hike would push many families and small businesses "over the edge," and blamed "Jim Chalmers's addiction to spending".

Pushed on whether the government could do more to meet the inflation challenge, Mr Chalmers conceded it had existed before the war in the Middle East.

"The best way to describe the inflation challenge right now is that we have an inflation challenge in our economy, made much worse by the war," he said.

He said while the government was committed to working on productivity gains, the benefits would "unfortunately" be felt in the "coming years, not necessarily the coming days and weeks".

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also blamed global inflation as the primary issue driving up interest rates, and acknowledged some people were "doing it tough".

"We'll continue to take work such as the $6 billion deficit compared with what was anticipated in our May budget," he said.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics is due to release the inflation figures for August on Wednesday.

title: Carpentry apprentice 'devastated' by CDU course delay
text:
An Alice Springs carpentry apprentice says he is devastated course delays at Charles Darwin University (CDU) could set back his qualification by up to a year.

Apprentice Lucas Nitschke said he hoped to complete his CDU TAFE carpentry course by the end of this year, however subject learning delays due to a staff shortage had pushed that out by up to 12 months.

Lucas Nitschke is a second-year carpentry apprentice. (Supplied: Lucas Nitschke)

"It's terrible, devastating, because it pushes back my work," Mr Nitschke said.

"This is my career. I sort of take this very seriously. I want to keep improving on my learning."

The university has been the subject of major accreditation, leadership and financial crises in 2026, including a course blunder that forced hundreds of tradespeople back to study and a directive to pay out more than $4 million in wages.

A CDU spokesperson said carpentry courses were being delayed again in Alice Springs because the qualified trainer was on "extended leave".

However, the ABC understands the lecturer has resigned from the position.

"Finding qualified replacement trainers is a challenge across the Northern Territory," the spokesperson said.

Problem after problem at CDU

It has been a tumultuous year for the embattled university.

In February, the ABC revealed a blunder in the TAFE's carpentry course, an error that would ultimately send hundreds of seemingly qualified tradespeople back to university to finish subjects.

The mistake led to the resignation of two high-level university figures later that month, including vice-chancellor Scott Bowman.

Former Charles Darwin University vice-chancellor Scott Bowman resigned from his role in February. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The university then halted a plan to open a campus in London, despite having already spent nearly $2 million on the proposal.

In June, the university was ordered to back pay more than $4 million in wages after it was found to have underpaid more than 800 employees between 2016 and 2022.

Last month, the NT government announced it was overhauling its partnership with CDU and would require it to abide by new key performance indicators.

In August, Jo Hersey announced CDU would face strict guidelines about how it spends government funds. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Education Minister Jo Hersey said she was in regular contact with the university and understood they were facing workforce challenges.

"To rebuild our economy and grow our skilled workforce we need a strong public training provider," she said.

" CDU is well aware of my expectations when it comes to training delivery. "

More students impacted

Mr Nitschke, a second-year apprentice, said the third block of trade school from September to October was cancelled just days prior to it starting, which was the second block to be called off this year.

The latest concerns raised by carpentry apprentices come amid a tumultuous year for the university. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

He said about 10 students were in a similar position.

"Being over halfway through my second year, I maybe have completed one unit block of my second year," he said.

"I'm basically nine months behind at least by now."

He said communication from the university had been limited.

"There's been nothing from CDU, honestly, [other than] just an email, there's just been no communication from them at all," Mr Nitschke said.

title: Madonna beats Taylor Swift in MTV awards showdown
text:
A battle between a 68-year-old pop icon and the most powerful woman in entertainment has ended in favour of the veteran at the MTV Video Music Awards in Los Angeles Monday morning Australian time.

Madonna took home three trophies including Artist of the Year, while Taylor Swift left with two, but one of them was the night's biggest prize.

Madonna led the nominations for the first time in 28 years, her 13 nods pipping Swift's 11.

Madonna's big night

Sabrina Carpenter joined Madonna to open the show with a version of Bring Your Love, their duet from Madonna's 2026 album Confessions II, which later won the Best Collaboration award on the night. Charli XCX then emerged to perform their track Danceteria Afterhours.

This opener won't grab the headlines like 2003's infamous kiss, but reminded fans and naysayers of Madge's continued skills as a performer.

Madonna beat just about everyone — Taylor, Sabrina, Ariana — to win the Artist of the Year award and backed that up with Best Dance to bring her haul for the night to three.

"Most of you were probably not born, but I performed at the first MTV awards 43 years ago," Madonna said in her speech accepting Artist of the Year.

As with any awards show, the night began with a focus on arrivals.

Here's what some of the stars wore on the red carpet.

Loading

Taylor Swift has the last laugh

While Madonna took home more trophies, Swift did get the big one, winning Video of the Year for The Fate of Ophelia.

Swift was also a record breaker before this year's ceremony even started.

Tied with Beyoncé at 30 wins apiece before the 2026 VMAs, she took the lead by winning the inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors, announced before the ceremony began. As a director, Swift has won four VMAs — more than anyone in history.

She used the moment to premiere the video for her song Patient Zero, featuring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell.

Swift left with two awards from her 11 nominations.

Snoop Dogg promises weed to winners

Snoop Dogg arrived on stage to rapturous applause and his song Who Am I (What's My Name)? from his 1993 album Doggystyle as the host of the awards show.

It was a sign of things to come, with Snoop classics playing in the background whenever he hit the stage.

"Welcome to the 2026 MTV VMAs," Snoop Dogg said.

"I'm your host with the most, the D-O-double-G Big Snoop Dogg."

Snoop Dogg hosted the MTV Video Music Awards held in Los Angeles, California. (Getty Images: Rich Polk/Billboard)

Snoop told the audience that Madonna killed it with her performance, which opened the show.

"Now, that is an icon," he said.

"One thing I want to say is, she ain't a virgin no more."

Snoop went on to say that when he was first asked to host the awards show, he asked if it would be in Los Angeles.

When the answer was no, that was his answer too, with the rapper telling organisers he was busy.

"Then they called me back and said, 'Hold on, Mr Dogg, It's in LA now.'"

Unless you've been living under a rock, you'll be well aware that Snoop Dogg is more than just a little bit partial to taking a puff or two of marijuana.

He went on to promise the biggest party the VMAs had ever seen, and some special "sticky-icky-icky" to the winners.

"But everybody else, look under your seat," he said before quipping.

"There should be nothing there."

Snoop gave a roll call of some of his "favourite people" who he said he was grateful to be in the company of at the ceremony.

"Madonna, Taylor Swift. Shaboozey, Lisa, Bruno Mars, and my girl, Raye, just to name a few," he said.

"Now, we got a lot of people in here tonight that's ready to party."

He also said the show would honour some of the most iconic bands and artists of all time including Nirvana, George Michael and Dolly Parton.

For his day one fans, Snoop harkened back to his Deeez Nuuuts skit on Dr Dre's The Chronic.

He then introduced Teyana Taylor to introduce the first award of the night.

Nirvana, Dolly Parton, George Michael honoured

If you need proof the VMAs is all about pop: this year they discontinued the Best Rock Video award.

Dave Grohl, Krist Novoselic and Pat Smear of Nirvana accept the Video Vanguard Award. ( Getty Images: Rich Polk/Billboard)

But the impact of grunge icons Nirvana defies genre, their Vanguard Award further evidence of their enduring influence.

"Their sound was loud, beautiful, daringly open," Public Enemy's Chuck D said when presenting the award.

"Their lyrics were poetic, raw and deeply human.

"Their music videos defined an era."

He called them "a band that changed the course of music" and that "never bent to the will of the mainstream", a stance that seemingly hasn't changed as guitarist Pat Smear smoked a cigarette on stage when accepting the award.

They weren't the only past legends honoured.

Sombr, Raye, and Teddy Swims delivered a high-energy tribute to George Michael, introduced by Canadian country star Orville Peck.

Kacey Musgraves performed I Will Always Love You in tribute to the late Dolly Parton, before Swift dedicated her Video of the Year award to the late country singer.

"Her storytelling was so vivid and so rich," Swift said.

"Listening to her songs is like watching the best music video you've ever seen in your life,"

Big, bold performances

VMAs performances tend to be far more interesting than the awards themselves, as artists leverage the big audience and production budgets to deliver spectacular displays of their visions.

From Madonna and Charli's bathroom stall choreography to Shaboozey's wild Western saloon, this year's VMAs pulled in a broad array of the current pop crop.

Blackpink star Lisa kept her Thai heritage front and centre in an epic performance of her new song Sawadika featuring some intense choreography.

British star Raye delivered a snippet of I Will Overcome before launching into a typically dazzling version of her hit Where Is My Husband!

Less impressive was Bruno Mars, who delivered a pre-recorded performance of Dance With Me, recorded on his current tour.

title: Hauser wins thrilling World Triathlon sprint, Parker breaks record
text:
Australian triathlete Matt Hauser showed he was up for the fight at the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Pontevedra, Spain overnight, beating Vasco Vilaça to the line in a thrilling sprint finish.

Defending series champion Hauser came into the series finale knowing he would be up against it to retain his title.

A number of crashes throughout the year meant Hauser needed to win and beat Vilaça by five places.

The Portuguese triathlete was in no mood to let the Australian get any sort of gap though, sticking with him through the swim and shadowing on the bike before the tremendous run stage.

"That's just ridiculous. I was just telling myself I can't lose this one, I can't lose this one," Hauser said.

"I've been so up and down this year and so inconsistent. I just really wanted it out there today.

"There is a lot to be thankful for and pleased for. I was really happy to get the win out there today and to execute when it really mattered.

"I'm not back-to-back world champion, but I can hang my head high. I achieved what I set out to achieve today and now looking onwards and upwards for next year."

Matt Hauser pushed the pace on the front during the run. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

Hauser and Vilaça ran away from Olympic champion Alex Yee, whose stunning run leg bought him into contention in the closing stages.

The Briton could not stay with the leading pair though as they engaged in what turned into a furious battle for the line.

Hauser's 'world champion persona' Despite being Australia's first male triathlon world champion in 20 years, Matt Hauser is still building the blocks towards his aim of Olympic success in 2028.

Both men were credited with a time of 1:39:31, but the Australian's dip on the line ensured he would claim victory by 0.08 seconds.

"Credit to Vasco, what a champion," Hauser said.

"I mean we got a bit pushy, shovy in the end. Apologies to him. I gave him a bit of a bump on my way through to get to the line first.

"[But] you have to do these things to get the victory sometimes, to have that dog in you.

"I didn't want to lose the sprint finish to Vacsco. I haven't lost all year to him.

"I have this notch in my belt this year and will take the momentum into next year and to LA2028."

Lauren Parker breaks record

Lauren Parker now has a record six world para triathlon titles. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

Lauren Parker also claimed victory in the PTWC race in Pontevedra, cementing her status as one of Australia's greatest-ever para triathletes.

PTWC events are for athletes who use a wheelchair in their daily life.

Racers in the PTWC category compete in a standard 750-metre open-water swim, but can use swim-exit handlers to help them out of the water. They then race a recumbent handcycle for the 20km cycling leg, before using a racing wheelchair for the 5km run leg.

The reigning Paralympic champion was never troubled in the race, leading from early on in the swim and thereafter, cruising to victory.

"I felt awesome out there in swim, bike and run," Parker said.

"I got a decent lead in the swim … I got on the bike and I felt so strong out there and I was pulling time into the girls, and extended my lead."

"And in the run, I was just holding them off."

The win secured the 37-year-old multi-sport star a sixth PTWC World Championship title.

It made Parker Australia's most successful ever Para triathlete, beating the legendary Bill Chaffey's previous benchmark of five world championship titles.

"It's just as special as my first title," Parker said.

"My first title was obviously [special because] it was my first. Number six means I've overtaken Bill Chaffey. It's awesome."

Parker won the PTWC class para-triathlon race at the Paris Olympics, having won silver in the same event in Tokyo in 2021.

She then backed up that performance to win para-cycling gold in the H1–4 road race and silver in the H1-3 time trial as well.

Not only that, but Parker can add four rainbow jerseys as a cycling world champion to her triathlon titles.

The Newcastle athlete also took to the snow in the past year, competing in both the biathlon and cross-country skiing at the Milano-Cortina Paralympic Winter Games in 2026.

Elsewhere, Anu Francis secured silver in the Women's PTS2 World Championship race.

The PTS2 classification is for non-wheelchair users for athletes who live with muscle power disorders or limb deficiencies.

title: Some farmers see nearly 100mm of rain in 24 hours in WA's south
text:
A weather system that formed in the north of Western Australia has made its way south over the weekend, bringing with it much-needed rain after a particularly dry winter, including one of the driest Julys on record.

In the Goldfields, Kalgoorlie-Boulder recorded four times its normal September rainfall, while some gauges in the south of the state recorded almost 100 millimetres.

Peter Buckenara farms grain and beef in the Bremer Bay region. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Bremer Bay farmer Peter Buckenara said it was the most rain he had received all year.

"We've had 78 mils at home here, and we've had 94 mils closer to town, so it's definitely been a very, very wet 24 hours," he said.

The beef and grain farmer said after 48 hours of constant precipitation, the heavy rainfall had damaged some crops, while other crops benefited from the rain.

"Unfortunately, the oats are lodged or fallen over, so it means they'll either have to be swathed, or we'll try and pick it up with a harvester off the ground," he said.

"Certainly a bit of damage there, but canola and wheat still looks fine."

Tributaries filled dams across the South West Land Division. (Supplied)

Balm for dry winter

As the state's grain harvest approaches, Mr Buckenara said he hoped for a break in the rain to give his crops and fields time to dry out.

"We're due to start hay early this week, and we'll certainly delay that just because the paddocks are too wet to get on," he said.

"We're probably a week away from swathing, so that might still happen on time."

Grain can clog machinery, and spoil if harvested when wet.

The state's south experienced a record dry July this year. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Bureau of Meteorology meteorologist Grace Abbott said the system that crossed the coast on Sunday night had largely dissipated, with conditions expected to dry later in the week.

"It looks to be light to moderate rainfall about the south coast for both Monday and Tuesday," she said.

"On Wednesday, we have a cold front brush by; it looks to be 1 to 5 millimetres, but some isolated 10 millimetres rainfall, particularly about the coast."

Grace Abbott says conditions will ease throughout the week. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

Conditions too dry

While it was a case of too much rain on the south coast, farmers about 200 kilometres north said much of the deluge fell around their farms rather than on it.

Gnowangerup farmer Timm House said he received 2mm on one property and 19mm on the other.

"We could see a lot of rain clouds went north and east of us [on] Saturday, and then Sunday we had a few showers go to the west of us," he said.

"We're hoping for a bit more than 2 millimetres [on the second property]. It would have been nice to get 10 to 15, that would have been awesome rain.

" But we'll definitely take the 19. "

Timm House is hoping for more rain. (ABC Great Southern: Rosemary Murphy)

Mr House said after a dry year that only saw the region crack about 200mm, he was hopeful about getting some rain ahead of harvest.

"We're still hoping the crops are going to be OK, but the rain that we've got over the weekend, wherever that fell will pretty much, barring no other issues, it will get us get us an average yield," he said.

"We would definitely take more rain."

title: Government delays Upfield line upgrades until 2033 with duplication promise
text:
The Carroll government will duplicate Melbourne's Upfield line if re-elected, but will delay scheduled works to remove level crossings for seven years.

The railway line travels through the northern suburbs and still has a section of single-line track between Gowrie and Upfield stations, limiting the amount of services that can be run on the line at any one time.

Premier Ben Carroll said the duplication would be crucial for Melbourne's north and improve reliability of rail services to the area.

"I'm from Melbourne's north-western suburbs; this has been spoken about for generations," Mr Carroll said.

Ben Carroll says residents on the Upfield Line have complained about long waits between services on the single-track line. (Flickr: Philip Mallis)

The premier estimated the duplication would cost between $650 million and $1.4 billion, but stopped short of guaranteeing funding for the project.

Instead, the government is financially committing tens of millions of dollars to a study of the potential duplication, if it's re-elected in November's state election.

"$80 million to do a detailed study on what the duplication will require, those four kilometres of track," Mr Carroll said.

"We will expect the planning and duplication study to be completed by 2028."

The premier says the Upfield Line will be duplicated by 2033 if he is re-elected this November. (ABC News)

When asked about the decision to spend $80 million on a study conducted by government departments and agencies, Minister for Public Transport Vicki Ward said it was a financially prudent investment in the future of Melbourne's north.

"The government is giving the money to the Victorian people and the people who live on this line," Ms Ward said.

The announcement is the latest in a protracted series of promised business cases and plans to duplicate the Upfield line.

In February 2025, the Albanese government announced $7.05 million towards delivery of a business case to develop and prioritise options for upgrades to Melbourne’s northern metropolitan railway lines.

In this year's 2026/27 Victorian state budget, the government allocated $3.6 million to "complete a final program business case" on improvements including duplicating the Upfield line.

Last year, the government's Big Build website had promised 110 crossings would be removed by 2030, a date which has now been delayed by a further three years. (Victoria's Big Build)

Now, the Carroll government's announcement has increased the spending on planning the duplication by nearly twenty-fold.

As part of the announcement, the government said it would also delay the removal of eight level crossings on the Upfield line.

Mr Carroll said the delays would align the work with the duplication of the line in 2033, saving $686 million.

The delays will further stretch out the timeline of the level crossing removal project, with the Labor government promising after its 2022 election victory that 110 removals would be completed by 2030.

Delays on Upfield line upgrades criticised by Coaliton, Greens

Shadow Minister for Transport Infrastructure Evan Mulholland lashed the government over the announcement, saying the government had now delayed the level crossing removal for two more elections.

"Not into the next term of parliament, but into the following term of parliament," Mr Mulholland said.

" Whenever this government needs somewhere to cut, it picks the Upfield line, and it picks the northern suburbs. "

Mr Mulholland accused the government of delaying the level crossing removals repeatedly as a political strategy.

"Why have they been delayed? Because this government needs to get them outside of the forward estimates, to not account for them," he said.

The Victorian Greens also criticised the announcement, saying the government had not committed to actually building the project and was delaying much-needed works on the line.

"Labor promised these level crossings would be gone by 2027. Then it was 2030. Now it's 2033 — while communities across the north continue to grow and wait for the infrastructure they were promised," Greens MP Anasina Gray-Barberio said.

"Communities in the north deserve so much better than empty pre-election announcements that just disappear over the horizon."

The Greens are calling on the government to commit $246 million to duplicate the Upfield line.

title: Sandon Smith leads Newcastle out of an Immortal shadow
text:
It's rare that anybody in Newcastle shares an accolade with Andrew Johns, but Sandon Smith has managed it.

Fresh off his electric double in the Knights' 22-14 win over Penrith on Sunday, Smith will join Johns as the only men to play halfback for Newcastle in a grand final.

"It's pretty cool to hear. I don't think I'm anywhere near that [Johns]," Smith said.

"But it's an honour."

Talking about Johns is part of the deal when you play halfback for Newcastle but it's wrong to compare the two because it's wrong to compare anyone to Johns, who stands alone as the club and the city's ultimate legend and hero.

Johns was more than just a player to the Knights, even if he's the best player they have ever had or will ever know.

The 1997 and 2001 premierships made Johns a Newcastle folk hero and the personification of the Novocastrian dream, larger than life through his greatness and profoundly human at the same time, like if they found a demigod in the front bar of a Cessnock pub.

Every Newcastle halfback since his retirement in 2007 exists, to one extent or another, in his enormous shadow which has a gravitational pull from which some players never escaped.

Andrew Johns remains Newcastle's greatest ever player. (Getty Images via All Sports: Chris McGrath)

You'd have an easier time replacing Christ in Christianity, because at least then there's supposed to be a second coming.

The only way to do it is to opt out of that framing altogether, because it's a game that cannot be won and therefore shouldn't be played.

Smith doesn't need to be Andrew Johns for Newcastle to make a grand final, the prelim is proof that being himself is enough.

His first try was a clever effort backed by his speed but his second, a length of the field intercept in the dying seconds that sealed the club's first grand final berth in a quarter century, was something else entirely.

It brought Johns himself to tears and for the post-Johns generation, many of whom are seeing the Knights in a grand final for the first time, it was the greatest moment of their supporting lives.

"The first one I was just trying to stay in the game and I saw an opportunity. Those don't always come off, but it worked well," Smith said.

"The second one, I didn't know if I could make it. My little legs were hanging on for dear life. But I was happy to make it, I'm ecstatic.

"It's hard to put into words. There's so much emotion going on.

"I think there was a few tears coming out. I was happy, I was tired, I can't really explain it.

"When I came to the club, I heard a lot about the town and how our football affects the town.

"It's hard to put into words when you're a part of it, but it's so true and it's so special, to be a part of something like this that is bigger than ourselves."

One of those supporters was Johns himself, who wept openly and spoke with a voice clouded with emotion on Channel Nine commentary in the aftermath of Smith's last score.

It was a gift of a moment, a slice of heaven wrapped in red and blue, the kind that Johns gave his team and his town back in those olden days, but until Smith went all the way the Immortal had never received it himself.

That alone would be a high honour, but Smith stood up multiple times on his team's biggest game since the Johns age, creating the break that led to Dominic Young's try early in the second half and forcing a key error from Lindsay Smith late on.

It sets up a grand final berth against the Roosters, where Smith played from 2023 to 2025 before he travelled to Newcastle in an effort for more NRL starts after the Bondi club signed Daly Cherry-Evans.

He insists there's no bad blood with the Tricolours as he tries to pilot the Knights to a premiership at their expense.

"It won't change anything for me. I'll enjoy it, I'll embrace this whole week. I'll stay in the moment. It's just another team and it doesn't change anything for myself or the team," Smith said.

"If we win a grand final, I don't think it matters who it'd be against.

"They were transparent with me [around Cherry-Evans]. I've got no remorse, I loved the club and loved my time there, but I'm a Knight now."

Like many of his teammates, Smith's been trusted to do more than one job this season.

He's at halfback now, in relief of the injured Dylan Brown, but has also spent time at five-eighth and as the bench utility.

Sandon Smith joined Newcastle this year from the Roosters. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

But he's played them all well and it's added up to the best season of his young career with Smith thriving under the coaching of Justin Holbrook, who he'd worked with as an assistant at the Roosters.

"Justo's been such a rock for me over the past few years, [especially] coming to the club with him when I was unsure about what this year would look like for me," Smith said.

"He constantly reassured me to keep my head down, keep enjoying myself and keep getting better.

"The NRL season is a long season and your moment will come. He kept saying you need to be ready when that moment comes."

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

All halfbacks wear pressure on their shoulders in grand finals and Smith does so with the added spectre of Johns's legacy.

But having already earned one opportunity that has eluded all other Knights halfbacks since Johns, Smith has a chance to win an even greater prize.

Newcastle's most glorious times are inextricably tied with Johns but now Smith and his teammates can write a new legend with victory on Sunday.

It is one which, for the first time in Knights history, can exist beyond Johns and his titanic legacy.

His shadow will always be longest, but now Smith and these Knights have stepped outside it they have the chance to cast one of their own.

title: Baird quits as CA chair as Big Bash sell-off fallout continues
text:
Mike Baird has sensationally quit as Cricket Australia chair, after his own state association refused to back its representative in the fallout over the privatisation of Big Bash League clubs.

The former NSW premier informed fellow board members on Monday he would not seek re-election at next month's annual general meeting, with David Boon to take over as interim chair.

The decision comes after Baird lost the support of Cricket NSW, with the country's most powerful state unhappy with the decision to allow private investment.

Baird had served as NSW's representative on the board, and approached it recently to confirm it would not support him in the current circumstances.

David Boon will step in as the interim chair. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

He did have the option of moving into an independent role, but AAP was told he did not wish to continue without the support of all states.

Cricket Australia (CA) officials maintain they continue to back the call for the privatisation of clubs, which was confirmed earlier this month.

"After much consideration I have decided to stand down as CA chair and director," Baird said in a statement.

"I am delighted that David Boon has agreed to undertake the interim chair role while we complete the formal chair process, and I will undertake a transition process with David over coming weeks."

Baird had been on the CA board for six years and had served as chair since February 2023.

Alongside Todd Greenberg, he formed one of the most powerful duos in Australian sport.

In a statement on Monday, he again referenced the privatisation of the BBL as a positive move for the sport.

"This year CA will report record revenue, profit, attendance and viewership, and most importantly a 40 per cent increase in participation over the past four years," Baird said.

"With recent decisions on the Big Bash I also believe the long-term sustainability is assured.

Baird's exit comes after Cricket NSW slammed the decision to allow privatisation earlier this month.

title: Knights star sent to NRL judiciary for tackle that broke Cleary's leg
text:
Phoenix Crossland will have to argue his case at the NRL judiciary if he is to have any chance of playing in the grand final after he was cited for the hip drop that broke Nathan Cleary's leg.

The Newcastle hooker was sent off during the Knights' thrilling preliminary final win over the Penrith Panthers on Sunday and the match review committee referred him straight to the judiciary.

Crossland landed on Cleary's lower left leg as the Panthers superstar took on the line in the 36th minute at Stadium Australia and was wrapped up high by Knights back rower Francis Manuleleua.

The injury was immediately visible, and Manuleleua quickly signalled for medical attention.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

As Cleary was receiving medical attention, including painkillers via the famed green whistle, replays on the big screen prompted Penrith fans and players to urge referee Gerard Sutton to send Crossland off.

Sutton called out Crossland and explained the incident in detail to him and captain Kalyn Ponga.

"Initially he's up high, he makes a definite action to twist," Sutton said.

"[He] comes down on the leg with weight, there's extreme risk of serious injury. You're off."

Crossland will need a miracle to play in the grand final.

Crossland was dejected in the sheds before his team pulled off a stunning 22–14 comeback win to reach its first men's NRL grand final in 25 years, but was greeted on the field after the game, embraced by a number of his teammates.

He seems at long odds to take the field in the grand final against the Roosters on Sunday.

Dragons forward Ryan Couchman was referred straight to the judiciary in round three for a hip drop that ended the season of Parramatta's J'Maine Hopgood.

Couchman was suspended for four games for the tackle that left Hopgood with a torn ACL after a 90-minute hearing.

"Whilst the panel accepted that this did not incorporate any element of intention or recklessness, it took the view that the player's level of culpability was significant, a factor reflected in the serious injury sustained by the ball carrier," judiciary chair Geoff Bellew said.

But earlier this season, Broncos hooker Cory Paix was not penalised or charged for a tackle that left Manly prop Siosiua Taukeiaho with a visible leg injury similar to Cleary's, breaking both the fibular and tibia.

"It's a horrible injury and I'm sure I speak for all Manly fans in wishing Siua a speedy recovery," Manly chief executive Jason King said at the time.

The Sea Eagles reportedly queried the decision not to cite Paix with the NRL.

title: Ireland refuses handshake with Israel, wears black armbands for game
text:
There were no handshakes between Republic of Ireland and Israel players before their contentious Nations League match, with the Irish team wearing black armbands for its 3–0 victory.

The game faced bitter opposition in Ireland over Israel's actions in Gaza, with the players coming under huge pressure to boycott their two matches against Israel.

Reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazuno left the squad for both games on the eve of the first match because of what he said was his "personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong".

The Irish players looked down at the grass with their heads bowed and hands behind their backs during the playing of the Israeli national anthem.

And Irish captain Dara O'Shea approached the centre of the field for the pre-match talk with match officials and his opposite number with his hands still firmly clasped behind his back.

Republic of Ireland captain Dara O'Shea (left) shook officials' hands but not Israeli counterpart Manor Solomon. (Getty Images: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile)

O'Shea shook hands with the referee and his assistants, but there was no attempt to shake the hand of Israel captain Manor Solomon.

There was a small group of Israeli fans in the otherwise almost-empty stadium in Debrecen, Hungary, but an even smaller group of around 10 people without colours were celebrating when Troy Parrott broke the deadlock in the 13th minute.

There were not supposed to be any Irish fans present. Some Ireland supporters who managed to get tickets through the Israeli soccer federation told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that those had been cancelled before the game.

A smattering of Israeli fans heckled and abused Irish players. (Getty Images: Ben McShane/Sportsfile)

Adam Idah made it 2–0 three minutes after Parrott's opener and Jack Moylan got the third goal in the 25th.

Ireland needed goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher at his best to deny Israel after the break, and tempers became frayed around the hour mark after a clash between Idah and Raz Shlomo.

Both players were booked by German referee Harm Osmers.

Israel forward Sayed Abu Farchi was suspended for the game after his sending off following his goal celebration in Thursday's 3–1 loss to Austria.

Ireland and Israel meet again on October 4 in Ireland's "home" game in Backa Topola, Serbia.

AI giant Anthropic will skip Thursday’s Senate hearing on rogue AI agents but send US and Australian executives to parliament next week. The hearings are the first chance for parliament to question the companies after an OpenAI agent got into a Medicare statistics portal in June without permission. Marles called it the first time this had happened in Australia. OpenAI did not tell the government for almost three months. Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei. Some of his staff are set to make upwards of $US100 million when the company goes public. Bloomberg Anthropic will appear before the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence on October 6, a source familiar with the matter confirmed. The company had asked the Senate’s environment and communications references committee for an alternative date, after being invited only last week to a hearing in Canberra this Thursday, October 1. Anthropic’s team is not in the country this week and cannot appear by video link because of an existing commitment, the source said. The company has told the Senate committee it wants to be constructive.

OpenAI has been contacted for comment but has not yet said whether chief executive Sam Altman, or anyone else from the company, will appear on Thursday. Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, who chairs the Senate committee, sent written requests to Altman and Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei at the weekend. Related Article AI Inside the elite meeting where OpenAI lectured on security, a day before the hack was revealed Hanson-Young said both men “must front up, face the Senate’s questions and have an honest conversation about what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should look like”. Shadow defence minister James Paterson has also called on the companies to make executives available to answer questions. Senate committees can summon witnesses and treat a refusal as contempt of parliament, but that power does not compel people living overseas. The committee could instead turn up the pressure on the companies’ Australian representatives, as this masthead reported on Sunday.

Advertisement

Anthropic’s local operation is run by Theo Hourmouzis, a former Snowflake executive who opened its Sydney office in April. OpenAI has no country chief based in Australia. Its most senior local figure is Brent Thomas, a former TikTok and Airbnb policy executive who leads its public policy work. Its new vice-president for Australia and South-East Asia, Sandhya Devanathan, is based in Singapore and is due to start in October. Theo Hourmouzis, general manager of Anthropic Australia leaving the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. James Brickwood Altman declined to answer questions from this masthead last week about whether he would apologise, or why it took months for OpenAI to tell the government. In a social media post on Friday (US time), he said: “We have not been as fast as we would have liked, but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes of agent activity logs, and working with impacted organisations.” OpenAI said on Sunday it had paused training of its latest models and would resume “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards”. It has notified dozens of organisations that its agents may have bypassed security controls, including US government agencies, and said most cases identified so far were “lower severity”. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said last week the agent had reached the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal and three other government sites through legacy systems linked to Services Australia. Defence Minister Richard Marles said the information obtained was “minor in its nature” and “wasn’t anyone’s personal data”. OpenAI has said it learned of the incident in August and that it was not intentional.

Advertisement

On Monday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese played down the seriousness of the medicare breach, stressing it was more about the implications for the future. “This doesn’t relate to people’s personal data, so what is at risk here isn’t what was obtained,” Albanese said at a press conference in Launceston, Tasmania. “It’s the way that it was obtained. [AI] can boost productivity, can boost economic growth, it can give us health breakthroughs, but we need to make sure that human beings are in charge of this.” OpenAI made a submission dated September 14 to the joint committee. It did not mention the Medicare incident. It did argue that “shared definitions, severity levels and reporting thresholds for significant AI incidents” would help countries respond together, and said OpenAI “would be pleased to further support the work of the Committee”. Anthropic has not been linked to the Medicare incident, but it has more riding on Australia, at least in the immediate term. It has signed a lease for the first stage of a $32 billion data centre at the Western Downs Digital Park near Dalby in Queensland.

It cited polling it commissioned from Pyxis Polling & Insights, which found 82 per cent of Australians were worried AI models would be developed overseas without having to adhere to Australian laws. Anthropic disclosed in July that its Claude models gained unauthorised access to three organisations’ systems during cybersecurity testing. OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are now investigating tens of thousands of incidents globally in which frontier models took problematic or unexpected actions. Both companies are negotiating with the federal government over access to Australian content to train AI models, in exchange for a greater local presence. The Commonwealth is also writing AI standards that will set mandatory requirements for large data centres. According to the Prime Minister’s department’s submission to the joint committee, the standards will include expectations for AI training developers on national security and safety. The joint committee is chaired by Labor MP Jo Briskey and has not asked either chief executive to appear.

Dateline Resources has landed heavyweight US Government backing in its fight to restart operations at its Colosseum gold-rare earths project in California, with two powerful federal departments throwing their weight behind the company’s push to overturn a preliminary court injunction. Judging by the market’s reaction today, this was just the tonic Dateline punters were looking for, with the stock rocketing a whopping 50 per cent to as high as 9.5 cents on turnover of 55 million shares in early trade. Dateline Resources’ Colosseum gold mine in California. The US Department of Justice has filed its own motion seeking a stay of the injunction that halted operations at Colosseum last month, while the Department of War has weighed in with a sworn declaration arguing that exploration at the project is in the national security interests of the United States. If granted, the stay would allow Dateline’s wholly owned subsidiary, Colosseum Rare Metals, to resume operations under its approved Plan of Operations while an appeal against the injunction works its way through the courts.

In its filings, the US Government has also requested the court allow Dateline to resume development work immediately while the stay order remains in place. The latest move follows an August 10 preliminary injunction issued by the US District Court for the Central District of California in proceedings brought by the National Parks Conservation Association. Dateline had already lodged its own application for a stay. The Federal Government has now joined the fray with a separate motion, arguing the District Court erred in finding that the “valid existing rights” savings clause under section 508 of the California Desert Protection Act did not protect an approved Plan of Operations. Importantly for Dateline, the Government is arguing that keeping the injunction in place causes irreparable harm to US national security interests and the broader public interest. That argument has been given some serious horsepower by Assistant Secretary of War for Industrial Base Policy Michael Cadenazzi, who pointed to Colosseum’s prime location just 10km north of the major operating rare earths mine at Mountain Pass and its associated processing facilities,

Cadenazzi said continued exploration at sites such as Colosseum was critical given the importance of rare earth elements to national security and America’s reliance on foreign sources. Mountain Pass, operated by mining behemoth MP Metals, is America’s only significant rare earths producer hosting a resource of 26.27 million tonnes at an impressive grade of 5.89 per cent total rare earth oxides (TREO). The next key date is October 26, when both Dateline’s and the Government’s stay applications are scheduled to go before Judge Christina Snyder – the same judge who issued the original injunction. Both the company and the Federal Defendants formally filed notices of appeal on September 22. Should the District Court knock back the applications, both parties can take their stay requests to the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. The broader appeal will continue in the Ninth Circuit regardless of the stay decision. The National Parks Conservation Association has indicated it will oppose the applications. The legal battle comes as Dateline looks to develop its 100 per cent-owned Colosseum project in California’s Walker Lane Trend. The company completed a bankable feasibility study on the project’s gold operation in May and has increasingly turned its attention to the site’s rare earths potential.

Advertisement

For the first time, Dateline has pulled all of Colosseum’s geophysical and geochemical data into one model, sharpening up three carbonatite-style rare earths targets. The standout is the 1.2km-long Clark Mountain Fault Zone, where electrical, radiometric, gravity and geochemical anomalies have stacked up in the same patch of ground. A second undrilled target on the eastern side of the project hosts a strong ring-like gravity anomaly, while a third target at 2200N is undergoing further modelling. Importantly, Dateline says the combined geophysical signature bears striking similarities to the nearby Mountain Pass carbonatite system. The geological case gained further weight when one hole at Clark Mountain delivered Colosseum’s first drill-based confirmation of anomalous rare earths, intersecting mineralisation about 40m deep on the edge of the priority target. Dateline says the rare earths signature and associated barium, strontium, calcium, phosphorus, thorium and uranium enrichment point towards a mantle-derived alkaline magmatic system comparable to Mountain Pass. Subject to the outcome of legal proceedings, the company now has a 12-hole diamond program lined up across its two leading targets, with several holes set to plunge beyond 750m in search of the heart of the interpreted carbonatite systems. Rare earths potential aside, the more developed gold story at Colosseum stacks up strongly. The previously published study presents what the company says is a technically simple restart of the historic mine with some hefty economics to match. At a base-case gold price of US$4200 (A$6000) an ounce, the numbers point to US$1.08 billion (A$1.54B) in undiscounted pre-tax free cashflow, a 49.5 per cent internal rate of return and a pre-tax net present value of US$785 million (A$1.12B).

Production is expected to hit its straps in year six at 102,000 ounces, while the operation is forecast to deliver 573,000 ounces across its 10.4-year mine life. title: Academics and heritage authority at odds over university building by NGV architect
text:

NationalVictoriaHeritage Academics and heritage authority at odds over university building by NGV architect Jackson Graham September 28, 2026 — 1:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A university building by the modernist architect who designed the National Gallery of Victoria is a step closer to the wrecking ball, after Heritage Victoria decided not to back it for protection. The University of Melbourne plans to replace the twin brick John Medley Building, which faces Grattan Street and forms a gateway to the Parkville campus, with a new central education building envisioned as a “welcoming front door” and “central hub for teaching, learning and campus life”. Academics have been pushing for the building to be on the Victorian Heritage Register, arguing it is a significant work by architect Sir Roy Grounds, who was a student at the university before building city landmarks such as the NGV and Arts Centre Melbourne. The John Medley Building was designed by Australian modernist architect Sir Roy Grounds and opened in 1971. Paul Jeffers However, Heritage Victoria executive director Steven Avery has recommended the site not be included on the register, and said the 1971 structure was “not a pivotal example of the class” of modernist postwar university buildings.

Advertisement

Avery said buildings such as the university’s Beaurepaire Centre and Wilson Hall, opened in the 1950s, were examples that defined the state’s modernist campus architecture and were on the register. “While the John Medley Building is a refined and attractive example of a postwar university building, it could not be considered architecturally notable when compared to examples already included in the [register],” Avery wrote. Grounds also designed iconic Melbourne landmarks including the Arts Centre Melbourne and the NGV. Mark Gambino The Heritage Council of Victoria, which has the final say, is yet to decide whether to grant the building protection and is currently assessing submissions, with the likelihood of a hearing that will delay an outcome until next year. Tony Lee, an expert on Australian modernist architects such as Robin Boyd, said Grounds knew the campus, where he had studied, lectured and served on the building committee, and the university handpicked him to design the building.

Advertisement

“He’s been very deliberately tying the building in with the university context, not just creating a building that is philosophically driven,” Lee said. Still, Lee said a key issue was a lack of documentation of Grounds’ work outside his designs in Melbourne’s arts precinct. “No one has put it in the context of his whole career. And I think it’s a very special building because, being a later building, it really shows the development of a mature architect.” The gateway created by the John Medley Building at the University of Melbourne. Paul Jeffers The John Medley Building, Lee said, incorporates medieval and Renaissance influences such as a walkway bridge that serves as a “gateway to the university” and thin windows that reference arrow slits. The slits lean into an Italian movement known as neo-liberty that borrowed from the past and foreshadowed postmodernism. “There are a lot of pure examples of all sorts of styles, but it’s these transition buildings that help tell the story to connect these periods,” he said.

Advertisement

“It’s probably the best building in Victoria and maybe even more widely in Australia of neo-liberty.” The National Trust is opposed to the demolition of the building on environmental grounds. Samantha Westbrooke, the organisation’s executive manager of advocacy and conservation, said the university should be doing more to consider the impact of tearing the building down. “We need people to be calculating the embodied energy that we lose when we demolish these types of buildings, and it should be factored into the demolition and rebuilding,” she said. “It’s more expensive from an environmental perspective, regardless of what you get at the other end.” An artist’s impression of the University of Melbourne’s entrance without the John Medley Building. The University of Melbourne spent $4.5 million refurbishing the building a decade ago. However, the plans to demolish the building were unveiled as part of a masterplan in 2023 that aims to “unite the campus with the city”.

Advertisement

The university’s chief operating officer, Katerina Kapobassis, said campuses needed plans for the long term “to meet the changing needs of research, teaching and students” while also “retaining their significance, layered history and connection to community”. Related Article Victoria residential property Inside the incredible Melbourne home of the architect who made the NGV More than 58 per cent of the university’s infrastructure comes under various heritage protection, and Melbourne University said it prioritised the conservation, adaptation and refurbishment of existing buildings. “However, where new development is necessary to meet functional and performance requirements, sustainability is embedded through integrated design, low-carbon outcomes, and a whole-of-lifecycle approach to materials, resources and environmental performance,” a university spokesperson said. “Redevelopment of the John Medley Building site will deliver a purpose-built teaching building that will become a focal point for student learning and community engagement at Parkville.”

Advertisement

A Heritage Council Victoria spokesperson said submissions were being considered on the building’s heritage status, and parties would be notified of any hearing scheduled. title: Wall Street’s multitrillion-dollar question: Could bonds end the AI boom?
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsBonds Opinion Wall Street’s multitrillion-dollar question: Could bonds end the AI boom? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 28, 2026 — 12:10pm

September 28, 2026 — 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The sudden spike in US bond yields over the past week to near 20-year highs raises a multitrillion-dollar question: Will those higher debt returns crash the sharemarket, and in the process derail the boom in artificial intelligence-related investment? Having edged up for most of the year – since the war in the Middle East caused oil prices to soar – the yield on US 10-year Treasury bonds has jumped from 4.95 per cent to 5.16 per cent in the space of a week, with similar moves across the yield curve. The spike in bond yields doesn’t bode well for the sharemarket, and its AI-investment boom. AP That’s the highest yield since 2007 on the 10-year bond – the global reference point for most interest-bearing securities – when it rallied in the lead-up to the global financial crisis. Bond yields and sharemarkets generally (there are exceptions) have an inverse correlation.

Advertisement

Bonds are “risk-free” assets. If you can get more than 5 per cent from investing in bonds, the dividend yield on the US stock market – currently about 1 per cent – starts to look unappealing when the risks of a sharemarket inflated by the hype around artificial intelligence stocks and trading at near-record levels are factored into decision-making. Higher yields push up borrowing costs, lowering company profits and dampening economic activity. They also lift the discount rates used to calculate the value of companies’ forecast future cashflows in today’s dollars. That’s a particular threat to an AI sector increasingly reliant on access to the debt market to fund the extraordinary levels of investment in chips and data centres, and the energy and water infrastructure to support those centres. There’s a lot riding on a continuation of the AI investment binge and the promises of transformative productivity gains being realised – for investors, and the global economy. The scale of the AI investments being made – in the US, it is more than $US700 billion ($990 billion) this year and could top a trillion dollars next year – and the rates of revenue growth that would be required to justify the investments are mind-boggling. They make the AI sector and the “hyperscalers” dominating the digital infrastructure, and accounting for about 35 per cent of the US market’s value, exceptionally vulnerable to an increase in discount rates.

Advertisement

So far, there’s been no material impact on the sharemarket from the spikes in yields. Apart from a brief sell-off when the US and Israel launched their attack on Iran in February, it has traded largely unaffected by the surge in oil prices above $US100 a barrel, the stubbornly high inflation rate and the US Federal Reserve’s decision this month to raise its policy rate for the first time in more than three years. Related Article Opinion

Global economy The four horsemen of the apocalypse are coming for the global economy That may be because of the continuing conviction that AI will change the world, and those companies leading the revolution will profit immeasurably. It may also be because the US economy is growing strongly, buoyed by the investment in AI, by fiscal stimulus – the US government deficit is running at almost 6 per cent of GDP – and the strength of spending by higher income households, and by booming corporate profitability. The AI investment boom may, however, taper or burst.

Advertisement

The resort to debt by even the hyperscalers – companies like Amazon and Alphabet – is an indication of the stresses even the biggest and most profitable companies are experiencing in funding their ever-escalating AI investments. Spending on AI has absorbed their vast legacy cashflows and is stretching the equity market’s capacity to support them with new equity. The rise in yields makes the cost of AI debt – which already has a risk premium – more expensive, while the rise in interest rates being driven by the bond market and the Fed will start to squeeze consumers’ finances. The spending by wealthier households has been held up, so far, by the Republicans’ tax cuts and by the wealth effects of the sharemarket boom. The rise in yields makes the cost of AI debt more expensive, while the rise in interest rates being driven by the bond market and the Fed will start to squeeze consumers’ finances. Corporate earnings growth has been exceptionally strong. Third-quarter earnings estimates put it at about 25 per cent of the same period last year. The earnings numbers are, however, inflated to some degree by the hundreds of billions of profits AI companies are reporting. Those profits flow from the markups in the value of their holdings in each other, in what’s been described as the “circular” AI economy. There’s a lot of paper profit and revenue within the sector.

Advertisement

At a macro level, the current US settings – the 6 per cent government deficit and more than $US40 trillion of government debt – are unsustainable in a rising interest rate environment. Related Article Opinion

Gold What the price of gold tells us about Trump and the future Peter Hartcher Political and international editor With the Fed having just started a rate-rising cycle and with the market pricing in at least three more 25 basis point increases over the next year, the threat posed to government and corporate finances by a rise in interest costs will only intensify. The US could grow its way out of the looming debt trap as low-cost debt issued in the post-financial crisis and pandemic eras continues to mature and be refinanced with higher-cost debt. But, more likely, it will have to try to inflate its way out, which will probably agitate the bond vigilantes even more. The risk to the sharemarket is heightened because today’s bond market is not what it once was.

Advertisement

Donald Trump’s trade wars and US sanctions have made the foreign central banks and institutions that were once the major buyers of US bonds more wary. They’ve been diversifying away from the US into gold and other assets. The market is now peopled by hedge funds and other traders, pursuing carry trades by either borrowing cheaply in other markets (Japan used to be the primary source of low-cost funding) or by running leveraged arbitrages between US physical bonds and their policing in futures markets. The risk to the sharemarket is heightened because the bond market during Donald Trump’s presidency is not what it once was. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson That makes the market more volatile and potentially vulnerable if an “event” causes the funds to suddenly unwind their trades. The bond market’s equivalent of the VIX index (often referred to as the “fear” index), which measures volatility in the sharemarket, is the MOVE (Merrill Option Volatility Estimate) index. It leapt over the past week from 78.56, which is roughly its average level of the past decade, to 96. Presumably, some of those leveraged bondholders became spooked by the pace of the run-up in yields.

Advertisement

With stocks trading at pricey levels – the cyclically adjusted profit-to-earnings or CAPE ratio is at levels last seen in 1999, in the lead-up to the bursting of the dot-com bubble – a sustained rise in interest rates is an obvious threat. It’s also a threat to both the real economy and the financial sector, where there’s been massive increases in non-bank, or “shadow banking” activity since the regulatory response to the 2008 crisis forced institutions out of a lot of financial market activities. Related Article Global economy The world economy is becoming wary of America There is perceived increased risk to the corporate sector and the economy being priced into markets, with the credit default swaps for investment trade companies blowing out and the yield curve in the bond market flattening. An index for insuring against defaults on US investment grade debt started the year at 51 basis points and is now at 58 basis points. Where it would have cost $US510,000 to buy insurance against a default on $US100 million of loans, it now costs $US580,000. For some of the hyperscalers, the cost is above 90 basis points, or more than $US900,00 per $US100 million.

Advertisement

The flattening of the yield curve – the difference between the yields on two and 10-year bonds has shrunk from about 85 basis points at the start of the year to about 30 basis points – indicates an expectation that the US economy will slow as the Fed, and the market, respond to the risk of sustained high inflation levels. It is, of course, conceivable that a sharemarket that has shrugged off Trump’s tariffs, the war in the Middle East and $US100-a-barrel-plus oil prices, $US40 trillion of government debt and the administration’s erratic policymaking can ignore the myriad of latent threats, buoyed by the transformative potential of AI. There’s a lot riding on a continuation of the AI investment binge and the promises of transformative productivity gains being realised – for investors, and the global economy. title: Treasurer Jim Chalmers touts stronger budget amid darkening economic outlook
text:
In brief Australia’s 2025-26 budget deficit came in about $6 billion better than forecast, driven by stronger investment and super income.

The improved result was overshadowed by expectations of a fresh RBA rate rise as oil prices fuel inflation fears.

Australia's budget has finished about $6 billion better off in the 2025/26 financial year, the government has revealed, as it braces for a damaging interest rate rise.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher touted their fiscal credentials when they released the final budget outcome on Monday, but also face difficult questions about an increasingly gloomy economic outlook.

Chalmers noted that today's improvements did not come from higher taxes on wages or commodities.

"Mining profits came in lower than what was anticipated," he said.

"It is overwhelmingly from higher super and investor income than what we anticipated in the Treasury's forecasts in May."

Though he readily welcomed the government's improved bottom line, he conceded there are "difficult months" to come, acknowledging that interest rates are expected to rise when the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) meets on Tuesday.

Gallagher confirmed the improvement to the underlying deficit, which was projected to be $28.3 billion in the May budget.

It's still a good deal worse than the previous year's final budget outcome, which put the deficit at just under $10 billion for 2024/25.

With deficits projected for another decade, and mortgage holders bracing for another Reserve Bank rate hike on Tuesday, Gallagher was forced to defend the role of government spending on inflation.

"We've found savings, including savings in an ongoing sense, to make sure that where government investment is happening, that it's not adding to the inflation challenge in our economy," she told ABC Radio National.

"But there is a war in the Middle East, and that war is having impacts not just at the petrol bowser, but across the board. The sooner that war ends, the better."

With inflation stubbornly above the RBA's 2-3 per cent target band, the Middle East oil shock is set to keep price pressures elevated for longer.

Brent oil futures lifted to US$106 a barrel as peace talks between the US and Iran hit another snag.

The shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, higher Chinese imports and softer exports from non-OPEC countries have further weakened the supply picture, said the Commonwealth Bank's head of commodities Vivek Dhar.

"If global oil and refined product inventories do deplete, Brent oil futures risk surging as high as US$150 a barrel to induce uncontrolled demand destruction (i.e. where high prices reduce demand) in emerging and developing Asian economies," he said.

Each US$1 increase in the Brent oil price roughly translates to a 1c increase in fuel prices at the bowser.

Those higher service station costs will likely nudge headline inflation from 3.5 to 4 per cent by the time the Australian Bureau of Statistics reports on Wednesday.

The US, Europe and Japan have all hiked interest rates due to rising fuel prices since the RBA met in August.

Hawkish comments from governor Michele Bullock and other top RBA officials in recent weeks have emphasised that the bank is losing patience with inflation and is likely to follow.

The bank's board is widely expected to lift the cash rate to 4.6 per cent when it wraps up its two-day meeting on Tuesday — the highest level in 15 years.

Liberal MP Zoe McKenzie sought to pin the inflation spike on government spending, despite growth in public demand moderating in recent years.

"The rest of the world is not experiencing the inflation that we are experiencing here at home," she told News24.

While drivers despair at the pump, auction clearance rates, a leading house price indicator, slumped to a 10-week preliminary low of 50.3 per cent on Sunday, according to housing data firm Cotality.

Median property prices nationwide have slumped 3.6 per cent since March's cyclical peak as the removal of tax concessions in May's budget combines with three consecutive rate hikes to cripple buyer confidence.

While Bullock has stressed interest rate decisions are not designed to target house prices, economists have linked lower house prices to consumers spending less across the board, tugging inflation down.

title: Does daylight saving mess with mental health? What to know before the clocks change
text:
In brief Daylight saving time starts on Sunday.

A new study examined how it affects mental health, amid overseas calls to end seasonal clock changes.

It's that time of year again. This weekend, millions of Australians trade an hour of sleep for more sunshine at the end of the day as daylight saving time (DST) begins.

For some, it signals the start of summery evenings in Australia and more light for after-work activities. For early risers, it could mean tougher wake-ups, with the sun rising later in the morning.

And then there's the disruption to sleep as the clocks move forward by an hour on Sunday — an adjustment often blamed for leaving people tired, irritable and out of sorts.

But new research suggests these disruptions don't necessarily translate into more serious mental health outcomes.

In an international review of existing research into a range of health and wellbeing effects associated with DST transitions, Swinburne University researchers focused specifically on outcomes including depression, bipolar disorder, dementia and seasonal affective disorder.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We found that there were no consistent or large effects on the transition to daylight saving time on these serious mental health outcomes," Ben Bullock, a senior lecturer and researcher at Swinburne University who specialises in psychology, sleep, mental health and circadian rhythms, told SBS News.

So what does that mean as the spring clock change approaches?

When does daylight saving time start, and where?

On Sunday 4 October, clocks in NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia, ACT and Norfolk Island will jump forward to 3am, costing people an hour of sleep in the process.

Queensland, Western Australia, Northern Territory, Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands do not observe daylight saving.

Daylight saving ends on Sunday 4 April at 3am, when clocks go back an hour.

New South Wales, Victoria, Australia, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory have all observed daylight saving since 1967.

Does daylight saving negatively affect your body?

Some sleep experts believe DST can negatively impact sleep, leading to other health risks.

Research suggests that sleep is crucial for mental and physical health, with chronic deprivation and disruption linked to mood changes, cardiovascular disease and impaired cognitive function.

The Sleep Health Foundation, for example, says DST can affect sleep patterns and overall wellbeing by disrupting the body's internal circadian rhythm and sleep-wake cycle.

According to the organisation, the springtime change of clocks is generally harder to adjust to than the one in autumn, when you gain an hour of sleep.

Sleep science organisations in the US, UK and Europe have previously called for seasonal clock changes to be abolished. In the US, President Donald Trump is pushing legislation to make DST permanent year-round across the country.

So, does daylight saving affect our mental health or not?

Bullock stressed the findings don't mean people can't feel the effects of the clock change.

Changes to the timing and availability of light can affect circadian rhythms and sleep, which can in turn influence mood and cognitive function.

But his research found little evidence that these effects translated into more serious mental health outcomes.

The review examined studies using hospital and other official records to measure serious mental health outcomes, including presentations involving depression, substance abuse and psychosis.

Bullock said the researchers wanted to examine whether the evidence supported significant policy changes such as the one proposed by several international sleep science groups.

"There are effects on sleep and circadian rhythms from changes in the available light and the timing of that light," he said.

"If we're going to get rid of something like daylight saving ... we need a stronger evidence base, and we just didn't find that it had that effect."

He said the broader review did, however, find small effects on some other health and wellbeing outcomes, including heart attacks and road accidents.

What can you do to get through the transition?

For those who struggle with the switch to daylight saving, Bullock said there are ways to make the adjustment easier.

In the days leading up to the change, he recommends gradually bringing your bedtime forward, rather than suddenly losing an hour on Sunday.

Getting outside into natural light early on Sunday morning can also help reset the body's internal clock.

"The third thing is to plan for the change and sort of be a bit gentle on yourself," he said.

"So don't plan any big things or big events, or expect to do lots of things on the Sunday after the transition."

"If you just look after yourself on that day, you will adjust slowly over the following few days. The body's pretty good at adjusting reasonably quickly, and it's quite resilient."
