title: Hundreds of dollars a year: How Tuesday's RBA decision could affect borrowers
text:
In brief The RBA is due to make its next rates decision at 2.30pm on Tuesday.

The call could send interest rates up for the fourth time this year.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is poised to make its next cash rate decision, with all major financial institutions agreeing that a rate hike is all but inevitable.

The 'big four' banks and financial markets have priced in an 80 to 90 per cent probability of a 25 percentage point increase, pushing the cash rate from 4.35 per cent to 4.6 per cent — its highest level since 2011.

The RBA is expected to view inflation risks as materialising faster and higher than previously forecast, demanding another rate hike.

The prolonged conflict in the Middle East, which has escalated and expanded in recent weeks, has pushed Brent crude oil prices to their highest level in months.

Domestic demand, GDP growth, and employment have proven to be far more resilient than expected, while Australia's productivity remains sluggish.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The latest figures, which will be updated on Tuesday, show headline inflation is 3.5 per cent, while the trimmed mean — a measure of inflation that removes the biggest price swings — sits at 3.6 per cent.

Fuel costs, housing construction, and dining out expenses are the main drivers of inflation at present, Australian Bureau of Statistics data show, pushing it well above the RBA's 2 to 3 per cent target.

Richard Witten, money expert at the comparison site Finder, told SBS News that Australia is at the mercy of "global inflationary pressures" with little agency over the issue, but that the RBA "has a mandate to keep inflation down" and that "their main tool for doing that is rate rises".

The big four predict the RBA decision

This is the first time in this current cycle that all four of Australia's major trading banks — Commonwealth Bank (CBA), Westpac, National Australia Bank (NAB), and ANZ — are forecasting a 0.25 per cent increase.

ANZ economists have said the RBA no longer views recent energy price spikes as a temporary blip, but as a broader, long-term inflationary risk they want to suppress. It has already predicted back-to-back rate rises, with another hike coming in November.

ANZ and the other big four banks are predicting the RBA will increase the cash rate for the fourth time this year on Tuesday. Source: AAP / Esther Linder

Westpac and CBA both brought their November hike prediction forward to this month. While they believe 4.6 per cent is the likely peak this cycle, both will be watching the RBA's explanation closely.

CBA said that if Tuesday's data shows a quarterly trimmed mean inflation rise of 1 per cent or more, a second rate hike in November will likely be triggered.

NAB said a single 0.25 per cent increase is the likely scenario, although a follow-up increase does remain a risk depending on labour data.

What another rate rise means for borrowers

If banks fully pass on the 0.25 per cent increase, borrowers can expect to pay hundreds of dollars more to service their loans.

The average home loan in Australia currently sits at $731,000, ranging from an average of $516,000 in Tasmania to $842,000 in NSW, according to ABS and Canstar data. First home buyers hold an average loan of $610,000.

The current average variable rate is between 6.24 and 6.62 per cent for owner-occupiers, meaning the average Australian is spending $4,500 to $4,680 per month on their mortgage.

A 0.25 per cent increase would add $120 per month to the average home loan, or $1,440 per year.

The average NSW borrower will pay an additional $138 per month, or $1,656 per year, while the average first home buyer will pay an additional $100 per month or $1,200 per year.

A 0.25 per cent increase also lowers the maximum borrowing capacity for new buyers by roughly 2 to 2.5 per cent, as bank serviceability buffers shift higher.

Renters are not immune, as property investors with variable loans are further incentivised to pass on these additional mortgage costs in a low-vacancy market where alternatives are scarce. The current national rental vacancy rate sits at 1.2 per cent.

Mortgage stress on the rise

Research from the polling group Roy Morgan shows that 29 per cent of Australian mortgage holders — around 1.54 million people — are currently classified as "at risk" of mortgage stress.

On average, servicing a new mortgage requires around 45 per cent of household income, up from 29.6 per cent in 2020.

Witten from Finder noted that while low interest rates were common around the globe for the decade or so before the pandemic, central banks are now raising rates to a "more historically normal" level.

"It's more challenging today though than in 2011," he said. "The amount you have to borrow now is much, much higher, so the same interest rate is much, much more expensive and punishing today than it was back then."

Finder's borrower survey data has not shown a major increase in mortgage defaults or distressed property sales, however Witten said that could change.

"The average borrower still has some sort of savings buffer they're relying on, but it does seem to be getting thinner," he said. "People will report higher feelings of mortgage stress, struggling to repay their home loan."

"They'll say to us in surveys that 'one more rate hike will put me over the edge'."

While the RBA is trying to keep inflation down, pushing rates higher risks triggering a recession as borrowers pull back on spending — something Bullock has previously noted the RBA is highly attuned to.

Witten said the central bank believes "borrowers can handle the hikes", but that a cash rate of 4.85 per cent may be as high as it's willing to go.

"Then it becomes a conversation around, 'does the government itself need to step in?' Because rate rises are just not working."

The RBA will announce its decision at 2.30pm on Tuesday, with Bullock holding a live media conference at 3.30pm.

title: A tiny camera. A hidden earpiece. And someone waiting outside the exam room
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

During the June exam period, University of Sydney student Charlotte (not her real name) left an economics exam relieved it was over.

She was already thinking about the exams she had left and the holiday that would follow.

Then she opened Douyin.

On the Chinese social media platform, she found a screenshot of some questions from the exam she had just sat.

The images were being used as promotional material by sellers of covert equipment, who claimed they demonstrated how their cameras could capture exam papers in real time from inside exam rooms. The University of Sydney later confirmed that material from 10 subjects had been leaked using hidden cameras during the June exam period.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Someone had posted some of the questions from the exam.

"The post had 'ECON1001' — the University of Sydney course code — written on it, along with hashtags for the university and 'final'," Charlotte tells SBS Chinese.

The "first-person view" exam footage promoted by sellers shows a question paper for a University of Sydney economics course. Credit: SBS

Charlotte had seen advertisements for the technology before — small cameras disguised as buttons, paired with wireless earpieces, designed to be used without attracting the attention of exam supervisors.

"Some of these cameras can vibrate. They can vibrate a certain number of times to indicate the answer choice," she says.

As technology makes it easier to capture and transmit exam material, universities face a new challenge: how to maintain exam integrity when questions can leave the room almost as quickly as students do.

Inside the exam cheating market

Following the University of Sydney exam leak, SBS Chinese searched Douyin using keywords including "Australian exams" and identified dozens of accounts advertising button-sized devices designed to secretly photograph exam papers.

Many accounts posted so-called "first-person footage" as a promotional tactic.

We approached five random sellers on the platform as part of our investigation. All said they could provide a complete cheating setup consisting of a button camera and a wireless earpiece "the size of a grain of rice", with the equipment available to either rent or buy.

Rental prices ranged from 3,000 yuan ($626) to 5,000 yuan ($1,044), while buying the equipment cost between 8,000 yuan ($1,672) and 11,000 yuan ($2,298).

One seller said: "The camera transmits the footage, while the earpiece is used to hear the answers. Once the camera captures the exam paper, we can see it on our end and then transmit the answers to you through the earpiece."

Button cameras marketed as tools for cheating in university exams are being promoted across multiple social media platforms. Credit: SBS

The seller said the students could either find someone themselves to answer the questions or pay an additional fee for "teachers who have graduated in the same discipline" to provide real-time assistance during the exam.

"Go with our teachers and the exam is guaranteed. Even though the University of Sydney has tightened its rules, our clients still pass," they said.

Another seller said the service would typically involve three "teachers" helping one student — two answering questions in real time and a third reading the answers to the student through the earpiece.

A third seller claimed to have sold more than 10 sets of the equipment in June alone.

The sellers assured the devices were "extremely discreet", with the camera designed to look like an ordinary button.

They also offered to provide training before the exam to show students how to set up the equipment and test that it was working properly.

Some sellers on select social media platforms are marketing high-tech cheating devices to students for use in university exams. Credit: Europa Press via Getty Images

The University of Sydney says it has made progress in its investigation into the June cheating incident, but declined to say how many students it is investigating.

A university spokesperson told SBS Chinese: "In this exam period and on previous occasions, we've identified a number of 'cheating jackets' with hidden cameras used to take photographs of exam papers, to be relayed via a connected device to someone outside the venue."

"These cheating companies are predatory and brazen. We've increased our support to students so they can seek help and report any approaches or suspicious behaviour."

The university said anyone found to have engaged in misconduct would face significant consequences under its disciplinary procedures.

How technology is changing exam cheating

Australia's higher education regulator says commercial academic cheating remains a persistent problem.

By December 2024, the federal government's Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) had blocked 422 websites offering illegal academic cheating services, including businesses that arrange for someone else to complete assessments on behalf of students.

Meena Jha, an associate professor at CQ University's School of Engineering and Technology, who has researched academic integrity in higher education, says the technology available to students is also changing.

She says new wearable technologies can include smart glasses, micro-earpieces and screen-enabled pens.

Associate professor Meena Jha says exam cheating has evolved alongside advances in technology. Source: SBS News

"If they are internet-connected, they can transmit data in real time while they are sitting, writing, doing the exam," Jha tells SBS Chinese.

It is real-time misconduct. It is not only one individual who is being involved here. It's probably the entire class.

Jha says the University of Sydney incident reflects a wider challenge for universities as the technology becomes more accessible.

"These technologies are available and as the technological costs are going down, they will be more available to our students," she says.

"These are quite alarming things and how universities are trying to grapple or to address these issues is a challenge."

The challenge is not limited to Australia. Regulators and education providers overseas are also dealing with the use of phones and other connected devices.

In the United Kingdom, exam regulator Ofqual reported 2,225 cases of student malpractice involving mobile phones and smart devices in tertiary and senior school exams in 2025, accounting for 44.3 per cent of all cheating cases.

The business after students are caught

For some students, the problems begin after the exam.

SBS Chinese found that after the University of Sydney exam incident, some academic appeals agencies started posting on social media, offering services to students facing university investigations.

These commercial agencies claim to help students accused of academic misconduct prepare for university hearings and appeals. Their services can also extend to other university matters, including applications to withdraw from subjects after the usual deadline, grade or assessment appeals, special consideration, and enrolment or course progression disputes.

But the services can be expensive, and the outcome is not guaranteed.

Faye (not her real name), an international student at Monash University, was one of those who sought help to improve her overall grade.

In January, concerned that a subject result could affect her future studies, Faye was introduced to an agency offering what it described as an "exceptional withdrawal" service.

She paid 4,500 yuan ($939).

Faye (not her real name), a student at Monash University, paid more than $1,500 for an academic appeals service, but her appeal ultimately failed.

The agency proposed that she apply for an exceptional withdrawal by providing medical evidence that she had experienced special circumstances while studying the subject.

"They said they had partnerships with local hospitals [in China], and that I could specify which hospital I wanted. They could contact them and arrange a certificate," Faye tells SBS Chinese.

The agency told her mental health issues were among the most common grounds for such applications.

They said, 'Because you were not in a good state and it affected your studies. That's the reason to apply.'

The medical certificate and its NAATI (National Accreditation Authority for Translators and Interpreters) translation cost an additional 2,750 yuan ($573), bringing the total to 7,250 yuan ($1,513).

The agency later told Faye that the university had changed its policy and would no longer accept medical certificates issued in China. Instead, she was required to obtain a certificate from a GP in Australia.

She then paid $45 out of pocket to obtain a medical certificate from a Melbourne GP and, with the agency's help, submitted the documents to the university. However, her application was rejected.

Why students seek outside help

Hongzhi Zhang, a senior lecturer at Monash University's Faculty of Education, who studied cultural perspectives in education, believes a lack of information is a primary reason students turn to commercial appeals agencies.

Universities generally provide students access to support and advice through their own services, but some students may not know those options are available.

Hongzhi Zhang, a senior lecturer at Monash University's Faculty of Education, says some students may distrust the support their universities offer and believe external organisations are better placed to represent their interests. Source: Supplied / Hongzhi Zhang

Zhang says some students may not trust the support their universities provide and may believe external organisations can better represent their interests.

He says students may also assume paying an outside organisation gives them a better chance at securing a favourable outcome.

"The internal support services are there to advocate for students and represent their interests. They can provide you with more accurate information, whereas external organisations may exaggerate the problem and make students even more anxious," he tells SBS Chinese.

Sometimes, students are looking for help in the wrong places. The first place they should turn to is the university, not outside agencies.

The price of an appeal

Sean Li is the founder of an education appeals agency based in Hangzhou, China. He graduated from RMIT University before completing a master's degree at Monash University.

He says his company was established about two years ago and currently assists between 30 and 50 students each month. His company charges around $2,000 for services related to academic misconduct cases.

Sean Li, the founder of an education appeal agency, says the industry aims to give students who have made mistakes a second chance. Source: Supplied

Li says they first help students determine whether their actions breached university rules before helping them prepare their appeal submissions.

We never help students fabricate anything. We don't make up facts for them either. If something didn't happen, then it didn't happen.

But he acknowledges questionable practices within the industry, including aggressive marketing, exaggerated claims about success rates, and in some cases, the use of fraudulent documents.

"Salespeople on the front end may sometimes over-promote the service when they're marketing it, and they may make excessive promises to clients about a particular outcome."

Li says he has also seen students obtain what were described as supporting documents from other agencies, some of which he believed were not genuine.

"If those documents are checked and found to be fake, the student could be in serious trouble. They could potentially be permanently expelled."

He rejects the suggestion that appeals agencies exploit the anxiety of international students.

He says the role of an appeals agency can be compared with the support universities themselves provide to students facing disciplinary processes.

We know students will make mistakes, and we're willing to give students another chance to continue their studies.

"The purpose of education shouldn't be for one failure to bring everything to an end. It should be about giving people who are willing to work hard a chance to keep moving forward."

A system under pressure

A TEQSA spokesperson told SBS Chinese: "TEQSA is aware that commercial academic cheating services continually evolve their strategies and services."

TEQSA published resources for students in November 2025 to help them prepare for and respond to academic misconduct processes.

"These resources support students to respond to allegations of academic misconduct without purchasing support from academic cheating services," the spokesperson said.

TEQSA said anyone who comes across advertisements for commercial academic cheating services or offers to provide access to assessment materials can report them to the agency.

Zhang says universities also have a responsibility to make their processes easier for international students to understand, particularly those from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds.

He suggests universities provide more multilingual services in addition to English, and include information about student support services when notifying students that they need to attend a hearing.

The emergence of these education appeals agencies is an opportunity for universities to reflect.

"If universities already have such comprehensive systems in place to support students, then why aren't students turning to you for help? Why are they going to external providers instead?"

Jha says universities also need to rethink how they design exams and assessments.

"If student assessment is no longer focused on rote memorisation, but instead on how knowledge is constructed, then these technologies can genuinely help students rather than being used for academic misconduct," she says.

She also recommends measures to detect Bluetooth signals and wearable devices during exams.

"There are some advanced smart gates available that can actually detect these devices when students are entering."

But she says there is a gap between rapidly evolving technology and the policies designed to regulate it.

Technology always takes a step and the policies follow it.

title: Rescuers race to find Australian hiker missing on remote Peruvian trail
text:
In brief Jordan Yap last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek.

Rescue crews completed their biggest day of search operations so far on Sunday morning (AEST).

Loved ones of a missing Australian trekker who was last seen nearly two weeks ago on a remote South American hiking trail are urging local authorities to help with the search.

A wide-scale sweep by a private rescue crew has so far failed to find any trace of 30-year-old Jordan Yap, who last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru's Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.

He was last seen near the start of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, regarded as a challenging, high-altitude route through the remote Andes.

Regarded as a very experienced hiker by friends and family, the Melbourne man failed to make contact on Wednesday, his estimated return date.

He also failed to check back into the Krusty Hostel in Huaraz, where his luggage remains stored, and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco on Thursday.

"It's really uncharacteristic of him to not have communicated at any point in his journey if he had the chance to," long-time friend Kevin Nguyen told the Australian Associated Press.

"It is a very popular trek, where you might have 200 to 300 hikers and guides per week during the busy season, so it is very uncharacteristic that no one's seen him since day one or day two."

The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.

Local mountain rescue organisation Socorro Andino Peruano has been hired by Yap's family to help with the search.

His loved ones hope the rescue group, which recently rescued a Canadian trekker from the same trail, can find him safe.

"Time is of the essence ... because ultimately, as much as we were saying he's been missing since the 23rd, he's had no contact with anyone since the 14th," Nguyen said.

Rescue crews completed their biggest day of search operations so far on Sunday morning (AEST), scouring various trails on the circuit to no avail.

"I know Jordan likes to orienteer and navigate and he's quite an adventurer himself, so I wouldn't be surprised if he tried an alternative route," Nguyen said.

Missing Australian hiker Jordan Yap (right), pictured with friend Kevin Nguyen during a previous hike of Mount Kosciuszko in Snowy Mountains. Source: Supplied, AAP / Kevin Nguyen

Yap had been planning the trek for more than a year and had recently bought a GPS watch to allow for offline maps to guide him on the hike.

"He was telling everyone about how he was ready to go on a big hike like this, (he was) really excited," Nguyen said.

He was last known to be wearing a white jacket, green sunshade sweater and grey pants.

The experienced trekker was believed to be carrying a 40-litre hiking bag, Durston dome tent and hiking poles.

Family and friends are urging the Australian government to work with Peruvian officials and local authorities to mobilise further resources in and around the rugged region.

The Australian embassy in Peru is helping his family.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

title: The cold drink stirring up a viral debate about professionalism
text:
In brief A recruiter in the US said Gen Z candidates are showing up to interviews with iced drinks and she perceives it as "too casual".

The take has proven divisive, with some agreeing and others viewing it as a dated idea of professionalism.

It's yet another debate dividing generations and the internet. At the heart of this one? Iced coffee in a job interview.

A recruiter's TikTok video has set off a viral online debate about whether it's appropriate to bring an iced coffee to an interview.

"My Gen Z candidates are showing up to their interviews with iced coffee, iced latte in hand," US-based recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen said in the video.

"It is perceived, from my opinion, my hiring standpoint, that when you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte that this interview is just like a stop on your list of errands on the day."

"It looks a little too casual to me," she added, advising candidates to finish their drinks before or after meeting with prospective employers.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While some commenters agreed that bringing an iced drink into a job interview was unprofessional and too informal, others argued it was an outdated and arbitrary way to judge a candidate.

"Are you expecting my whole day to revolve around a 30 min meeting?" one commenter wrote.

"As a millennial, can we please let go of the weird rules boomers and Gen X imposed on us? Interviews are stressful enough," said another.

"It's not about coffee it's about professionalism," another commented. "Surprised people aren't getting that."

Wehniainen later joked on LinkedIn that she had accidentally started a national debate and her comment section had become a battlefield.

She said she was "never saying that bringing coffee makes someone a bad candidate".

"My point was simply about avoiding distractions."

An industry insider's take

Amy Slade-Symons has been a career coach for around 10 years and worked in talent recruitment and HR for more than a decade before that.

She told SBS News she personally wouldn't bring a coffee into a job interview, but it also shouldn't be a big deal if you do — as long as you're on time.

"It's just always is bad form if you turn up late, no matter what, and you're holding some form of drink in your hand," she said.

She noted, though, that she can't speak for everyone, and different hiring professionals have different biases.

But "if the candidate makes a great impression — skills, experience, motivation for the role, what they can bring — I think that eclipses most things", she added.

Government analysis suggests young people face an increasingly difficult path into the workforce, with the transition from education to employment becoming more complex and many entry-level roles ultimately going to more experienced candidates.

Australia's workforce is more generationally diverse than ever, with four generations working alongside one another.

With Generation Alpha beginning to enter the workforce in the coming years, that could soon become five.

That brings different communication and leadership styles, expectations around formality and workplace attire, and approaches to learning together in one place, Slade-Symons said.

She has seen those expectations change significantly over her own career.

"I've gone from wearing a suit, stockings, full face of makeup, through to going into the office wearing trainers and a nice frock and maybe a business jacket over the top if I'm having a formal meeting," she said.

"You interview people now, and I might be online wearing a hoodie because that's the environment that they work in, or wearing a T-shirt."

As workplace norms evolve, she said it's easy to look at younger generations and think: "In my day that was different."

When it comes to iced coffee, her advice is that it's probably not worth risking it, even if it feels silly.

"Get their focus on the conversation about your skills and experience and how wonderful you are."

text:

Fans revelled with the team at the Brunswick Street Oval.

Celebrations were ongoing on Sunday after the Brisbane Lions pulled off a three-peat in a nail-biting AFL Grand Final.

title: Flood disaster declared in Bangkok after more than 300mm falls in monsoon deluge
text:
Key Points More than 300mm of rain has fallen on Bangkok in 48 hours, causing flood across the city.

A flood disaster was declared across the city, and the prime minister cut short a trip to London.

Bangkok authorities declared a flood disaster across the Thai capital on Saturday after almost 48 hours of heavy rain left homes, shops and roads waterlogged and residents wading through waist-deep water.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul cut short a trip to London to return home after more than 300mm of rain fell in some areas between Thursday afternoon and Saturday morning, according to officials.

"The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now," said Somkid Pheuk-ngam, 67, a vendor who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok.

"I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now," she told AFP.

Bangkok is no stranger to wet weather, and September is the peak of the rainy season, but several residents said it felt worse than usual.

"I feel like in all the many years I've lived here, I've never encountered anything like this, where it rains continuously for days," said 63-year-old resident Anutin Meechamnan.

The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) declared a disaster across all 50 districts of the city, a move that grants local organisations special powers to act.

READ MORE Why scientists are collecting orangutan poo deep in the Borneo jungle

Bangkok governor Chadchart Sittipunt said on Saturday afternoon that the situation had "stabilised", adding: "If more rainwater doesn't fall in the area, it will be solved."

"If the rain stops, it is expected that it will take two to three days to drain the floodwater," he said in an update broadcast on social media.

Temporary shelters

Almost continuous rain since Thursday afternoon has swelled Bangkok's network of canals, sending murky water into surrounding homes, restaurants, shops and alleyways.

"Our problem is that the canals are full," Chadchart said.

"We are cooperating with nearby provinces and try to drain water out through other sides, minimising the amount that flows into Bangkok."

Bangkok is built on former marshland and rests about 1.5 metres above sea level.

READ MORE Two years on the run, these parents teach survival skills no child should need

The BMA said earlier that the city's pumping stations were operating at full capacity, drawing a combined 1,200 cubic metres per second.

AFP reporters saw residents wading or pushing their motorcycles through high waters in several districts of eastern Bangkok, while parked cars were partially submerged on one major road.

In Bang Bua district, a woman tried to salvage goods from her shop as the floodwaters rose to her thighs.

Khem Amnueilaph, an office worker who lives in Suan Luang district in eastern Bangkok, said the water in his neighbourhood was "higher than knee level".

"My house is new so it was elevated, but some old houses nearby the water have already flooded," the 36-year-old told AFP by telephone.

"I have food in my stock for two to three days, but I may have to wade through the floodwater for food later," he said, adding: "I have no idea how to get to work on Monday."

Some convenience stores were out of stock by lunchtime as residents raced to buy essentials.

Chadchart said at least 13 major roads were flooded but urged residents not to worry about potential food shortages, stressing: "The public doesn't have to be panicked."

He said around 980 people were staying in temporary shelters, while authorities had transferred 36 bedridden people to hospitals. The city has also prepared one million sandbags.

Despite hopes that the water will recede, Bangkok authorities said schools would close on Monday, while some officials have been asked to work from home.

September has been wetter than usual, according to figures from Bangkok's drainage and sewerage department.

The capital recorded 487mm of rain between 1 and 25 September compared to an average of almost 269mm for the same period from 1991 to 2020.

Scientists warn the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events will increase as the planet continues to warm due to fossil fuel emissions.

Flooding was also reported on Saturday across 21 provinces in Thailand, according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation, with more rain expected on Sunday.

Widespread deluges across the country in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes.

title: Migrants are sending billions overseas. What does it mean for Australia's economy?
text:
In brief Remittances have become a contentious point in Australia's migration debate.

Critics argue they drain the Australian economy, while proponents say the provide a crucial lifeline to family abroad.

Remittances have become a talking point in Australia's migration debate.

Some anti-immigration activists argue remittances drain money from the Australian economy, while others say that view ignores migrants' economic contribution and the support these payments provide to families overseas.

So what's the real impact — both for the economy and for migrants and their families?

Mrinaal Datt, who moved to Australia from India four years ago and is the founder of Indian Women Abroad, regularly sends money back to India — often a few hundred dollars at a time.

She told SBS Examines that the remittances went towards her partner's parents' medical expenses.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"In Indian and a lot of South Asian cultures in general, they have a saying that you don't just marry a person, you marry the whole family," she said.

"It's not just you and your partner. It's your siblings, your parents, their parents. You can't think of not supporting your family. It's just not comprehensible to an average person who comes from India.

"It just feels like it's your duty as a child to support them through all their medical procedures."

A Money Transfer Australia report said $35 billion was sent from Australia as remittances in 2024, including nearly $7 billion to India.

"When someone earns that money in Australia, but remits part of that portion overseas, that portion is not being spent here," political commentator Jaimie Johnstone said in a recent social media post about the report.

"That money is not going to an Australian cafe or restaurant. It's not being spent with an Australian tradie, it's not being used to purchase Australian products, not in an Australian shop, not circulating within an Australian household.

"And if we're going to have a serious national conversation about immigration, surely capital flowing out of our domestic economy should be part of that conversation too."

But Ryan Edwards, an associate economics professor at the Australian National University, says we should be sceptical of these numbers.

"We don’t really measure money going out very well ... those numbers are actually much softer," he said.

Even if those estimates were correct, "that would still be under 1 per cent of our economy" and tax had already been paid on the income.

He noted the argument against remittances didn't account for the benefits migrants bring.

"The real counterfactual here is one of a migrant versus no migrant," he said.

"You take away that person, yes, you've stopped the money from flowing out, but you've also stopped all the jobs, the wages that they spend here, often on things that Australians are producing, and the tax that they've paid.

"We know that most migrants tend to be net positive fiscal contributors."

Muhammad Omair Ziaee is a technology and healthcare entrepreneur of Pakistani heritage. He sends money to his family and employees back home in Pakistan, but he says most of the money his businesses make is spent in Australia.

"If we compare to the money which we're sending over ... that's under 20 per cent of what we actually earn and what we spend over here," he said.

Remittances part of culture

Supriya Singh, an adjunct sociology professor at La Trobe University, said money is "one of the foremost ways" to show care in many cultures.

"If you come from China, you come from Vietnam, you come from any part of the Middle East, you come from the Pacific; sending money home is a way you tell your family that you belong, that you're thinking of them, that you care for them."

She said care was expressed differently across cultures.

"Across the world, it's the people who do not send money home that are in the minority," she said.

However, Singh said remittances can be used as a tool for financial abuse, noting the issue came up during Victoria's Royal Commission into Family Violence.

"When a person is using them not for care but for appropriation. If the parents demand too much of the child and the child does not have enough money for his or her own settlement expenses, then remittances can become a medium of abuse," she said.

Strain on already tight budget

Datt from Indian Women Abroad said remittances are a cultural practice but can strain already tight budgets.

"I think parents have to realise is that your child is not your retirement plan," she said.

"Everyone who comes abroad knows that it is really really hard when you're paying for the university fee. So many people are living paycheque to paycheque. It really is like a cultural thing. I actually hope things will change for the next generation."

She added her contributions to Australia outweighed the remittances back home.

"If you think about all the money that we spent, the flights that we paid, the income tax that we pay, our rentals, our mortgage now, I think we've spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in Australia," she said.

"The $200 or $400 is sent back home. That's nothing in comparison."

According to a World Bank estimate, global remittances to low and middle-income countries reached $924 billion in 2023, and continued to be "essential drivers of economic and human development".

title: US and China agree on 'super intelligence' label for AI, cut tariffs by $42 billion
text:
In brief The US and China agreed to cut tariffs on $42.6 billion worth of goods and establish a new trade council.

The two countries will also launch formal AI talks, including a channel to manage AI-related incidents.

The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on US$30 billion ($42.63 billion) of goods and launch a dialogue on AI, both countries said following President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington.

The tariff reductions would apply to US exports such as agricultural goods, wood, and cosmetics, as well as US imports, including small appliances, toys, and decorations, a White House statement said on Friday, local time.

"The two countries reached consensus on recommendations for more favourable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction," the White House said.

The three-day summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump, which ended on Friday, showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs. Xi has since landed in Beijing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.

The two sides also agreed to establish a trade council and to extend the outcomes of earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, the Chinese foreign ministry said.

title: Jane Hume says 'we're missing the point' on OpenAI Medicare breach
text:
In brief Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has criticised the government's response to the OpenAI Medicare breach.

It comes after the government suggested taking legal action against the US-based ChatGPT developer over the incident.

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has accused the federal government of "missing the point" in its response to the OpenAI Medicare breach, arguing the incident exposed serious gaps in Australia's cyber defences.

The government is examining whether those involved in the breach could be prosecuted under existing Australian law.

Environment Minister Murray Watt said a task force investigating the incident was seeking advice on what action was possible under current laws and whether changes were needed to deal with similar incidents in the future.

Speaking on ABC's Insiders on Sunday, Hume said the "real alarm bell" was that the government only became aware of the hack because OpenAI disclosed it.

"I'm not entirely sure who they're going to put into cuffs," she said. "I think we're missing the point here."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"If they hadn't of told us that there was a breach, would we have known about it at all? That demonstrates that our cyber defences, particularly for [Services Australia], was woefully inadequate."

She questioned whether OpenAI was at fault, adding, "the idea that we would only check an inbox once a day when that inbox is specifically set up to identify cybersecurity breaches is mind-boggling".

Her comments follow Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's revelation this week that an agent linked to OpenAI, the California-based developer of ChatGPT, gained unauthorised access to Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

Both the government and OpenAI have said no personal information was accessed during the breach, but it has raised broader concerns, including over the time it took to report it and who is accountable.

The 18 June incident was reported to Services Australia by OpenAI on 10 September, when the company emailed a Services Australia inbox.

Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said that inbox is typically used by researchers to alert the government agency to possible vulnerabilities in its systems, and is only checked once a day.

She said the email was discovered the next day and escalated on 15 September after checks to determine it was legitimate.

She said she was notified on 17 September. Albanese disclosed it publicly on 24 September.

PM says incident was not isolated

There have been dozens of cases of artificial intelligence agents wrongfully accessing classified information beyond Australia's Medicare hack, Albanese said on Saturday.

But he said he wasn't aware of them before revealing the unauthorised OpenAI infiltration of the Medicare Statistics Reporting portal while in New York on Thursday.

"At the time we made our announcement ... we weren't aware of other occurrences," the prime minister told reporters on the tarmac at Sydney airport.

"We were acting purely in our national interest."

Albanese returned to Australia after a week in the US, where he addressed the United Nations General Assembly on the international need to rein in AI.

He now says news that rogue AI agents hacked into US government websites is further proof of that need.

Autonomous agents are now known to have infiltrated US university and commerce department sites, as well as the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

"We now know it wasn't just the issue of the Australian sites that have been subject to AI agents accessing information without authorisation," Albanese said.

"What this does is confirm that approach of making sure that it needs to be an appropriate national response, as well as an international response to make sure that humans are in charge of this new and emerging technology."

Albanese said it was up to OpenAI to state why multiple breaches occurred.

Albanese spoke with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman by phone while in New York, with the tech boss admitting the company had not done enough.

An OpenAI spokesperson said, “Yesterday we announced we've paused training our most capable models and will resume training them only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards and alignment improvements in place, which we are working on now."

Australia is among more than 20 countries that signed a joint statement calling for cooperation to establish global AI standards and ensure human control.

However, US President Donald Trump used a speech at the UN to lash out at calls to put the brakes on AI.

title: Donald Trump rejects Iranian peace offer, says US is 'winning tremendously'
text:
In brief US President Donald Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal to end fighting in the Middle East.

Iran raised the proposal at the United Nations on Friday.

US President Donald Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the Middle East.

Iran raised the initiative at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the US via Qatari mediators and that it could reopen the strategic waterway and put an end to hostilities in the region within seven days.

But in comments to reporters at the White House on Saturday, Trump said: "I reject their proposal ... I rejected their deal."

"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they're losing so badly," he said before leaving for Tennessee. "We're winning tremendously.

"They want to make a deal and I think that's fine, I like making a deal too. What they want to do is immediately open the Hormuz Strait ... because they have no money coming in, because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait," Trump said.

title: Emma's relationship ended. Now, she's caught in Australia's $2bn debt battle
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

This article contains references to family and domestic violence.

When Emma's relationship ended, the financial uncertainty didn't.

She says her former partner's child support payments became inconsistent, leaving her struggling to rely on the money she was entitled to. It forced her to rethink how she could protect herself and her child.

"I couldn't rely on the payments coming through," Emma tells SBS News.

There were elements of domestic violence, emotional abuse and coercive control behaviours.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

SBS News has withheld her surname for privacy reasons.

In a bid to protect herself and her child, Emma switched to Agency Collect, the government's Child Support Scheme (CSS), where Services Australia collects payments on behalf of separated parents.

For 18 months, Emma was receiving the child support she was entitled to — until the payments stopped.

She says her former partner took advantage of a "loophole" in the system and registered themselves as "self-employed" to avoid paying the amount she says was owed.

As of March 2026, almost $2 billion in child support debt was owed by parents using Agency Collect.

As of March 2026, outstanding child support debt among parents using Agency Collect stood at almost $2 billion. Source: iStockphoto / Tolikoff Photography/Getty Images/iStockphoto

A Department of Social Services (DSS) spokesperson told SBS News: "The amount of unpaid child support in this country is utterly unacceptable ... This is parents robbing their children of the support they need and in many cases leaving them to live in poverty."

But that figure only captures debt recorded through Agency Collect. It does not include unpaid child support under private arrangements between parents, meaning the full scale of the problem is unknown.

Emma's experience raises questions about how Australia's child support system responds when payments stop and what happens when financial control continues after a relationship ends.

How Australia's Child Support Scheme works

The CSS was introduced in 1988. It was designed to create a national system for assessing and collecting child support, with the aim of ensuring separated parents contributed financially to the cost of raising their children.

The scheme initially relied heavily on compulsory collection, including through wage withholding, where child support could be deducted from a person's salary.

However, by the mid-1990s, the scheme was reformed, giving parents greater choice over how their child support was collected.

Professor Kay Cook is an associate dean of research at Swinburne University of Technology, who specialises in child support policy. She says the reforms reflected a view within the government at the time that the system was "too onerous" on fathers.

They gave parents more choice, and it was all done under the rhetoric of making it easier and fairer ... but it returned all the power to the fathers.

Cook argues the changes shifted greater responsibility for managing child support onto parents, while government policy at the time emphasised giving separated parents more choice and flexibility in how payments were arranged.

For separated parents, there are two main routes for child support payment.

The first is Private Collect, a personal agreement in which payments are handled by the two parents without Services Australia collecting or monitoring.

Child support can be handled privately between separated parents or collected and managed by Services Australia through Agency Collect. Source: Moment RF / krisanapong detraphiphat/Getty Images

The second is Agency Collect, which is organised and overseen by the government through Services Australia.

There are 1.2 million Australians who have a child support arrangement — with 590,300 actively using Agency Collect.

The $1.99 billion owed by parents using Agency Collect does not capture those with Private Collect arrangements.

SBS News understands there are currently 229,355 non-paying parents — and only 59.4 per cent of them have an active repayment arrangement.

"We have no idea what is happening in the other half," Cook says, referring to Private Collect arrangements.

She believes the amount would be much higher.

Does the debt signal a bigger issue?

The debt is a result of an "underpayment of the amount that is meant to be paid in child support", according to Cook.

She says it most commonly occurs when the paying parent declares they are self-employed or "choose to pay or not pay when they want".

"People manipulate how much they pay, through working cash-in-hand jobs, or keeping their own business," she says.

They make their taxable income look really small.

Cook says there are little to no repercussions, describing Services Australia as a "toothless tiger".

In 2025, the Commonwealth Ombudsman investigated complaints about Services Australia's response to withheld payments and what it described as the "weaponisation" of child support.

The investigation found that Services Australia was "not doing enough to identify and respond to financial abuse through the Child Support program" and lacked "policies, strategies and training to be able to proactively identify, monitor and respond to cases of financial abuse".

A 2025 Commonwealth Ombudsman investigation found Services Australia was not doing enough to identify and respond to financial abuse through the Child Support program. Source: Moment RF / Kseniya Ovchinnikova/Getty Images

These findings prompted an Australian National Audit Office audit of Services Australia's child support debt-recovery enforcement powers. The findings are scheduled to be tabled in November 2026.

It's estimated that almost 100,000 parents using Agency Collect have experienced or are at risk of experiencing family or domestic violence.

Cook says the CSS operates under "the assumption that parents are equally bargaining and making decisions".

"But, in family violence ... when a perpetrator can't physically control you anymore, the number one tool they have left is to financially control you."

Adrianne Walters, executive director of Women's Legal Services Australia, says the "deliberate nonpayment of child support is economic abuse".

"It takes food off the table, destabilises households, and it punishes children in order to control their mothers," she tells SBS News.

The body recently surveyed 540 separated mothers, finding that 80 per cent reported experiencing financial abuse via the CSS.

Walters says the body regularly witnesses "women exhausted by the process".

"Years of underpayment and mounting debts, and the stress of other legal processes while the child support system asks them to keep pursuing a person they might be frightened of. Many simply give up," she says.

While the child support system has provisions intended to protect people experiencing family and domestic violence, Cook says they fail to account for the nuances of financial abuse.

"You have to prove it, and the system knows what to do with physical abuse, but it's not very good at recognising coercive control and financial abuse," she says.

[The CSS] is compelling women to be tied administratively to their abuser for decades.

"Instead, lots of women are just going to Private Collect and aren't collecting anything."

Do the new reforms actually fix the problems?

In the 2026-27 federal budget, the government announced a landmark $182.6 million investment over four years to reform the CSS.

The reforms include removing the requirement for certain personal financial information to be automatically shared with the other parent, increasing discretionary powers to limit harassment and harm between parents, expanding wage withholding and introducing a new Collection Arrangement Guidance Tool for new parents entering the CSS.

The government will also "strengthen data sharing" between Services Australia and the Australian Taxation Office and "prosecute people who don't lodge their tax returns to avoid their child support responsibilities".

From 1 July 2027, the government plans to automate the issuing of Departure Prohibition Orders (DPOs), a legal tool used by authorities to prevent people with significant unpaid debts from leaving the country.

That will include automatically issuing DPOs to some parents with child support debt of at least $10,000 who have travelled overseas more than once in the previous two years.

"We believe that if you can afford an overseas trip, then you can afford your child support," a DSS spokesperson told SBS News in a statement.

In the 2025-26 financial year, 672 DPOs were issued, according to the government. It expects the reforms to result in an extra 3,000 DPOs being issued in the first year.

Reforms will be legislated "progressively, with the first tranche to be introduced in parliament in the coming weeks", the spokesperson said.

Cook says the changes are "underwhelming" but are the "beginning of system change".

Walters noted that while they're the "most significant action taken against systems abuse in recent history", they fall short and do not fully address the experiences of parents in Private Collect arrangements.

She hopes to see the changes implemented with the safety of victim-survivors as a priority, and stronger access to free, specialist legal support for women to navigate the system safely.

"We need action to stop perpetrators from forcing women into Private Collect arrangements — like making Agency Collect the default arrangement until certain safeguards are met," Walters says.

"These actions must be accompanied by stronger accountability for deliberate non-payment ... better options for reviewing and enforcing Private Collect arrangements, so non-payment doesn't disappear from view."

The child support system means Emma will remain financially connected to her ex-partner until their child is at least 18. Credit: Christopher Hopefitch/Getty Images

Like many parents using the CSS, Emma will remain connected to her ex-partner until their child is at least 18 years old.

Believing the insecurity of payments kept her in the "cycle of abuse", she's worked hard to no longer be reliant on child support.

It came with significant sacrifice.

Sometimes you might have to ask people, your family, for help. You have to cancel things for yourself that might help your mental health.

"You might have to find housing in a non-ideal area because it's all you can afford, and you might have to work and juggle more.

"It's just part of the sacrifices you make as a parent — you put your child first."

title: Brisbane lions win AFL Grand Final in nail-biting finish against Fremantle Dockers
text:
In brief The Brisbane Lions are the 2026 Grand Final winners.

A couple tied the knot outside the stadium ahead of the match.

Brisbane have become the third team this century to claim an AFL premiership three-peat after beating Fremantle by seven points in an all-time classic grand final.

Fremantle led by 17 late in the game and were on course for a maiden premiership when Brisbane burst to life and Logan Morris put the Lions in front with a minute left, then kicked the sealer.

In prevailing 14.12 (96) to 12.17 (89) in front of 100,023 fans at the MCG, the Lions join Hawthorn (2013-15) and the legendary Brisbane team of 2001-03 to win three premierships in a row this century.

Two final-quarter goals from Logan Morris sealed victory for the Lions.

The Dockers pulled the trigger on their "Wharfie Time'' crowd activation when Patrick Voss put them up by 17 points, before Brisbane reeled them in, delivering coach Chris Fagan a third premiership amid heavy speculation it was his final game at the helm.

Brisbane midfielder Will Ashcroft (31 disposals, nine clearances) and co-captains Harris Andrews and Josh Dunkley were fantastic, along with forward Charlie Cameron (three goals) and veteran Dayne Zorko.

Charlie Cameron kicked three goals in the Lions' third straight AFL flag.

Brisbane champion and former Docker Lachie Neale, who contentiously had his one-game striking ban overturned at the AFL appeals board on Thursday, was heavily booed by the Fremantle fans throughout.

Heavy rain on Saturday morning meant covers were on the ground before the pre-game entertainment, headlined by Kylie Minogue, but the weather cleared up ahead of the main event

They love each other — and they love the Fremantle Dockers

On AFL Grand Final day, a couple from Western Australia took their commitment to both to the next level, tying the knot outside the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) ahead of the 2026 AFL Grand Final match-up against the Brisbane Lions.

Matt Abbott, Danni Bloomfield and their celebrant — a close friend — were all smiles as they performed the ceremony, clad in purple Dockers scarves over their wedding attire.

"I love you, and I will always be in your corner. I promise to stand by you through every Dockers game," Bloomfield said during her vows.

"Go Freo!"

Bloomfield told ABC News they had planned to get married and then "walk straight in and go and watch them bring home the cup". She said she even ordered a purple dress, but it didn't arrive in time.

The couple flew to Melbourne from Karratha to watch their beloved Dockers face the Lions. Source: SBS News

The couple, who have been together for 15 years, had been planning to throw a surprise wedding at Bloomfield's 50th birthday party, but pivoted at the last minute when their team made the final.

Their celebrant Luke Lalor told the ABC he'd never done a wedding with 100,000 guests, and thought it was a "fantastic" idea that they were marrying "exactly where they want it".

Bloomfield and Abbott are among thousands of Dockers and Lions fans who have travelled to Melbourne for the big match.

Pop superstar Kylie Minogue dazzled in an upbeat pre-game show, belting out hits such as Can't Get You Out Of My Head, Spinning Around and Padam Padam.

How did Brisbane and Fremantle get here?

Fremantle beat Brisbane 103-78 when the sides last met at the Gabba in May, at one stage leading by 51 points.

Dockers Jye Amiss and Patrick Voss kicked four goals each, while Josh Treacy added three.

Freemantle finished the home-and-away season as minor premiers, while Brisbane secured a top-four finish.

Neither side took the direct route to the grand final, with both losing their qualifying finals before fighting their way back.

Brisbane lost its qualifying final to the Sydney Swans by 53 points, then recovered with victories over the Adelaide Crows and Hawthorn Hawks to reach their fourth consecutive grand final.

Fremantle suffered a 72-40 loss to Hawthorn before bouncing back with wins over the Geelong Cats and Sydney to book a place in the final.

Brisbane won three consecutive premierships from 2001 to 2003, while the Dockers have never taken home the cup since entering the league in 1995.

title: Donald Trump praises Xi Jinping as US visit wraps up, but little progress on key issues
text:
In brief Chinese President Xi Jinping has wrapped up a three-day visit to the US.

US President Donald Trump praised the visit but no agreements were reached on major issues.

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping drank tea at the White House and visited the National Archives on Friday local time, ending a three-day summit that showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs on a host of contentious issues.

Trump said "our farmers are going to be happy" as a result of the talks but did not provide details.

"America is very happy about this visit, and I'm sure China is very happy also," he said.

Xi said the US-China relationship had developed into a constructive one of "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity".

The summit between the world's two largest economies featured military flyovers, ceremonial tours and a state dinner, but left unresolved major differences over trade, artificial intelligence, Taiwan and China's ties to Iran. Details of the limited trade agreements reached during the visit will be released on Monday, US trade representative Jamieson Greer said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

One tangible outcome of the visit was that the US and China agreed to extend by two months a trade truce that was due to expire on 10 November, allowing more time to work on ‌a potentially bigger trade deal.

Greer told CNBC that the US has agreed with China to exempt some key goods from trade disputes, including exports to China of agricultural products and medical devices, and imports of consumer and non-sensitive goods.

Trump highlighted progress under a bilateral trade mechanism, citing increased market access for US farmers and ranchers, while both leaders identified AI as an area for dialogue.

"In some ways, the best thing that we accomplished in this visit is to continue the conversation," US ambassador to china David Perdue told Fox News on Friday, local time.

Trump announced in a social media post that he and Xi would meet twice more this year, in China in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and in Miami in December at a G20 summit.

"Much has been, and will be, accomplished," Trump said.

National archives tour

After tea in the White House Red Room, Trump and Xi rode in limousines to the National Archives, where they reviewed the US Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights.

Asked about Iran, Trump said he and Xi had discussed it and that "I think we're going to do great," without elaborating. China has denied US allegations of helping Iran's leaders in the conflict launched by Trump in February.

Perdue said in an interview with CNBC on Friday that Trump reiterated to Xi that direct or indirect support for Iran was "totally unacceptable" and received assurances that China would not do so.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Thursday that Xi had urged the US and Iran to return to negotiations to end the war, but Xi has not publicly commented on Chinese support for Iran.

China presses on Taiwan

A key issue for Xi was the status of Taiwan.

China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own, and Xi has long sought to persuade Trump to state publicly that the US opposes Taiwan's independence, rather than merely saying it does not support independence, which has been the US's formulation for decades.

He also wants the US to halt arms sales to the island.

Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan on Thursday, saying he hoped the US would "handle the Taiwan question with prudence".

China's state news agency also reported that Xi "hopes the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing 'Taiwan independence'".

While the US, like most countries, has no formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, Washington is its most important international backer and is bound by US law to provide it with the means to defend itself.

The US's Asian allies were watching closely to see how Trump talked about Taiwan following Xi's visit. As of Friday afternoon, he had said nothing substantive.

After his May summit with Xi, Trump, whose administration in December approved a US$11 billion ($15.6 billion) arms sale package to Taiwan, said he was holding a second package, worth some $14 billion, in abeyance and described it as a "very good negotiating chip".

On Thursday, Democrats criticised Trump for failing to publicly address China's military pressure on Taiwan and called for the immediate delivery of approved military aid and arms sales to the island.

title: ‘Comprehensively bad thing to do’: Why we should stop putting data online
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Hacking attacks have become so common that keeping data safe feels like an impossible task, with some cybersecurity experts saying the system is "fundamentally broken".

Mihai Lazarescu worked for years as a 'white hat' hacker finding vulnerabilities in computer systems, and says organisations simply don't have the resources to effectively manage the threats.

The cyber security consultant, who is an associate professor at Curtin University, says news this week that Australia's Medicare statistics portal was hacked — the first known hack of an Australian government website by an agentic AI agent — is another example of the challenges involved in keeping data secure online.

While no personal information was believed to have been accessed, it follows major data breaches involving businesses including Origin Energy, Optus and Medibank in recent years, in which personal data was accessed or stolen.

"My experience dealing with different organisations — ranging from small businesses to banks — is that they struggle to find enough resources to cover [cyber security]," Lazarescu tells SBS News.

Even if they have the funds to protect their systems, finding people with the right skills is difficult.

The reality is that if people want to get to your data [and] it is available, they'll probably find a way to do it.

Lazarescu says continuing to place data online at the same rate "makes no sense" and the system is "fundamentally broken".

"We can't protect things, and now you have this emergence of automatic agents, why do we keep going it?"

Lazarescu says consumers need to push for change.

"If there's no pushback, this is going to keep going."

Should we go back to paper records?

In recent years, there's been a trend towards putting everything online, but given the security risks, Lazarescu questions why it's necessary for businesses, especially telcos and power companies providing essential services, to store their customer data on the internet.

These businesses have millions of customers, which means a cybersecurity breach has the potential to impact significant numbers of people.

Almost 10 million people had personal information accessed in 2022 when Optus' system was hacked, and around 10,000 had their data published on the dark web.

Customer data of mobile phone service provide Optus was compromised after a cyber attack in 2022. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

The hack of Origin Energy in July impacted almost one million current and former customers.

The number of hacking attacks is rising, with the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner saying it received 1,205 data breach notifications in 2025, an increase of 8 per cent from the previous year.

Until a system is developed that enables information to be stored securely, Lazarescu says some businesses should consider returning to paper records, something that was functional in the past.

I've seen all kind of benefits being touted [to putting stuff online]. I haven’t seen yet any evidence that [it's] paying off.

Lazarescu points out the internet is essentially "unsecurable", arguing its underlying protocols were designed in an era when computers were primarily being used to link academics at different universities and assumed users were trustworthy.

"At the fundamental level [it] can't be secured unless we have an internet 2.0, and I can’t see anybody trying to do that," he says.

This makes putting stuff online a "comprehensively bad thing to do".

But Rahat Masood, a senior lecturer at the School of Computer Sciences and Engineering at the University of New South Wales, is sceptical about whether returning to paper records is practical.

She says technology has advanced and a significant increase in printing could also increase carbon emissions.

"The only solution I can see is public awareness and sharing less data, and companies collecting less data," Masood tells SBS News.

Rethinking data collection

While companies should be minimising the amount of personal information they hold, they often have limited incentives to delete data once it has been collected. Masood says many companies earn money from selling data.

It’s now common for businesses to ask for personal details from customers even when some of that information may not be essential to providing the service.

Masood points to Medicare card details being stolen during the recent Quest Apartment Hotels data breach.

Why do you need the Medicare [details to rent an] apartment?

The Quest hack raises questions about not only what information businesses collect, but also how long they retain it. Some impacted customers told the media they had last interacted with the business years ago.

Masood says data should only be stored when it is needed, and then deleted after a certain time period, including when a person dies.

While fines of up to $2.5 million for a person, and up to $50 million or other substantial penalties for a company, depending on the circumstances, can be issued for privacy breaches in Australia, Masood points out that laws are often not enforced.

She believes companies operating in Australia should be audited to ensure they are meeting the requirements of the Privacy Act 1988. This regulates how government agencies as well as some organisations, including those with an annual turnover of more than $3 million, handle personal information.

Changes should also be made so that people are given user-friendly and concise information about companies' privacy policies, instead of pages of terms and conditions they don't understand.

Masood says customers need simple information about what type of data is stored on business servers, how it is used, why it is needed, the potential consequences of this data storage, as well as who they can contact with issues.

"It's not a difficult task, it's just that companies don't want to do it."

More accountability needed

Jacqueline Boaks, a lecturer at Curtin University who specialises in business ethics, says there's often a sense of inevitability around AI and a sense of powerlessness that anything can be done to stop it, but she argues that societies have well-established laws to hold people morally and legally responsible for creating and releasing a product that does harm.

"We shouldn't forget that, just because something's digital and not physical," she tells SBS News.

We as a community and as the government need to have an expectation morally and ethically around who is accountable and who is responsible when [hacks] happen.

Boaks says it's impossible for individuals to oversee how their data is managed by companies or to opt out of services such as Medicare.

"[This] is a pretty vulnerable place to be, but it does seem to be exactly the kind of thing that we have a right to expect governments to protect us from," she says.

"That's one of their core roles."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese indicated support for regulating artificial intelligence at an international level during a speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week. Source: AAP / Sarah Yenesel/EPA

But Boaks says there's often a disconnect between the level of harm done through these data leaks and the consequences faced by companies.

Lazarescu agrees the consequences are not serious enough for companies to change their practices.

What happens when you have a breach? Do you see anything in terms of people being held accountable? Organisations being held accountable?

Lazarescu, who grew up in Romania under Communist Party rule, is also sensitive to what could happen if more aspects of people's lives move into digital systems, particularly if governments can easily erase people.

"To me the biggest problem with putting stuff online is that you can also modify it online."

What can people do to protect their data?

Leaders such as United States President Donald Trump have rejected the need for stronger AI regulation, and Trump has also criticised Australia's plan for digital duty of care laws that would give residents the option to opt out of algorithmic feeds.

But Lazarescu says this doesn't mean every American agrees with the Trump administration's position.

People have a lot more power and they need to be engaged and tell the politicians enough is enough.

At an individual level, Lazarescu and Masood warn against sharing anything online unless it is absolutely necessary.

This includes posting on social media, which can allow companies to build detailed profiles of users, avoiding unnecessary sharing of documents such as passport copies, and not entering sensitive details into AI programs such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and other large language models.

"It's very crucial now," Masood says. "You need to be minimising the data yourself."

title: Anthropic boss to skip Senate grilling into rogue AI agents
text:
